title: Temporal Feasibility and the Limits of Resource-Based Economics

detail.title: Temporal Feasibility and the Limits of Resource-Based Economics

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: Traditional economics typically treats resource feasibility as the fundamental condition for the existence of economic states. Once resource constraints are satisfied, the corresponding economic state is generally assumed to be attainable in principle. However, many failures observed in real economic systems do not arise from the absolute absence of resources, but from the inability of processes to be completed within given temporal structures. Supply chain congestion, institutional delays, financial rollover failures, and coordination bottlenecks demonstrate that economic states may fail to emerge, persist, or complete even when resource conditions remain satisfied. This paper argues that resource feasibility does not automatically imply realizability. Conventional analysis often relies on the implicit relation: s ∈ E R ⇒ s realizable The paper further discusses the implications of this framework for equilibrium theory, growth theory, and institutional capacity analysis, and argues that economics must move beyond resource allocation alone toward the analysis of realizability under temporal constraints.

title: The Theory of Privacy Interests: A Heideggerian Onto-Epistemological Perspective Toward Privacy Actions
affiliations: Indiana University, Virginia Tech, Virginia Tech - Pamplin College of Business and Virginia Tech - Department of Business Information Technology

detail.title: The Theory of Privacy Interests: A Heideggerian Onto-Epistemological Perspective Toward Privacy Actions
detail.abstract: Prevailing information privacy theories have advanced understanding of how users evaluate privacy risks. Yet, they leave important aspects of user behavior insufficiently explained, particularly why some consumers proactively protect their personal information, whereas others remain passive despite expressing similar privacy concerns. Much of this research relies on privacy concerns as the primary indicator of privacy attitudes. Privacy concerns are crucial, but they largely capture users’ risk-focused evaluations of data collection, use, and disclosure. They therefore explain how users react to perceived privacy threats better than how users develop sustained engagement in protecting their privacy. We propose and test the Theory of Privacy Interests to explain this consumer-side engagement. By privacy interests, we mean users’ experiential engagement with protecting their personal information—the extent to which privacy protection is meaningful to them, they feel competent to pursue it, and they believe their actions can influence privacy outcomes. This construct refers to users’ privacy-protective interests, not to the economic or strategic interests of firms, platforms, or other producers that supply privacy-adjacent digital environments. Drawing on the Heideggerian onto-epistemological framework, we conceptualize privacy interests as experience-based, skillful engagement with privacy protection that develops through users’ repeated interactions with digital environments, privacy risks, and privacy-protective practices. We empirically examine privacy interests and privacy concerns as distinct but complementary constructs. Across three scale-development data collections and four survey studies with 3,922 participants, we find that privacy interests are more effective in explaining proactive privacy actions. In contrast, privacy concerns are more effective in explaining reactive privacy actions. This research operationalizes the Heideggerian onto-epistemological framework to shift attention from users’ risk evaluation to users’ sustained engagement in actualizing privacy protection. In doing so, our research offers a complementary explanation for variation in consumer privacy behavior and advances research on privacy attitudes, privacy actions, and the privacy paradox.

title:
Digital Chokepoints and Sanctions Regimes:

Rethinking International Law Frameworks for Critical Digital Infrastructure in the Strait of Hormuz

detail.title:
Digital Chokepoints and Sanctions Regimes:

Rethinking International Law Frameworks for Critical Digital Infrastructure in the Strait of Hormuz
detail.abstract: The expansion of global digital infrastructure — particularly submarine cable networks — has fundamentally redefined the geopolitical calculus of the twenty-first century. The Strait of Hormuz, long recognized as the world's foremost energy chokepoint, has simultaneously emerged as one of the region's most sensitive digital communication corridors. This article adopts a critical-analytical approach within the field of international technology law to examine the tension between two foundational principles: freedom of global communications as a core value of international law, and the imposition of technology sanctions regimes against states that occupy strategically critical positions along this infrastructure. The central argument is that the current technology sanctions regime is not only incompatible with the principles of internet governance and the regulations of the International Telecommunication Union, but actively endangers the stability of global digital infrastructure. The article concludes by proposing a five-element legal framework for more equitable governance of critical digital infrastructure in strategically significant geographic regions.

title: P-hacking and Policy Arbitrage under a Data Disclosure Mandate: Evidence from the Journal of Accounting Research
affiliations: Fudan University,  and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - Lingnan (University) College

detail.title: P-hacking and Policy Arbitrage under a Data Disclosure Mandate: Evidence from the Journal of Accounting Research
detail.abstract: We examine how mandatory data disclosure affects p-hacking and provide evidence of policy arbitrage: authors with stronger pre-policy tendencies to report just-significant results become more likely to publish in peer journals without equivalent disclosure requirements. Using the Journal of Accounting Research's (JAR) 2014 data-disclosure requirement as a quasiexperimental setting, we find a significant decline in just-significant reporting in JAR relative to the Journal of Accounting and Economics (JAE) and The Accounting Review (TAR), two comparably prestigious outlets that had not adopted such policies. Consistent with policy arbitrage, this effect is driven primarily by a decrease in such reporting in JAR alongside simultaneous increases in JAE and TAR. We further show that, after the policy's adoption, authors with a stronger prior tendency to report just-significant results become more likely to publish in JAE and TAR rather than in JAR, and that their papers are a key driver of the postpolicy divergence across journals. Overall, our evidence suggests that disclosure policies can be effective within adopting journals, but their broader effects may be attenuated when peer outlets do not adopt similar standards.

title: RESISTÊNCIA DISCURSIVA E SUBVERSÃO COLONIAL EM PAPÉIS DA PRISÃO DE JOSÉ LUANDINO VIEIRA

keywords: discursive resistance; hidden transcript; colonial subversion; José Luandino Vieira; Frantz Fanon; James C. Scott; Angolan prison literature

detail.abstract: O presente artigo analisa os Papéis da Prisão de José Luandino Vieira (2015) como paradigma de resistência discursiva anticolonial, a partir do cruzamento analítico de dois quadros teóricos complementares: a distinção entre discurso público e discurso oculto proposta por James C. Scott (1990) e a teoria das três fases do intelectual colonizado formulada por Frantz Fanon (1961). O argumento central é que os Papéis da Prisão operam simultaneamente em três registos de resistência discursiva: a condição material dos cadernos como discurso oculto produzido à margem da vigilância colonial; a subversão da língua portuguesa a partir de dentro, mediante criolização com estruturas do quimbundo; e a conversão do texto íntimo em projecto de consciência nacional, correspondendo à terceira fase fanoniana do intelectual que «compõe a frase que exprima o povo». A análise demonstra que a especificidade da resistência de Luandino não reside no confronto exterior com o colonialismo mas na sua infiltração e subversão interior, uma forma de resistência que o colonial state reconhece, ao proibir o texto, como mais perigosa do que a recusa aberta

title: Developing Employability through Education Imperative for New India

detail.title: Developing Employability through Education Imperative for New India
detail.abstract:
Human capital is the accumulation of investment in people. The most important type of human capital is Education in the form of acquiring certain threshold competencies. It represents an expenditure of resources at one point in time to raise productivity in the future. Investment in education is tied to a specific person. Acquisition of knowledge and skills through education can make a person employable in Industry. Educational systems of any country have a direct bearing on the quality of Human Resources it produces.

Employability can be broadly defined as the ability of a Person to get employed, who is qualified and ready to work, having Competencies (Knowledge, Skills and Attitudes) matching with Job requirements of Industry.

Any educational system normally not only should make people literate but make them gainfully employed post-knowledge/ skill acquisition. Firms use educational attainment as a way of sorting out between high-ability and low-ability Employees. This implies, when person earn a university degree, he not only become more productive, but also indicate his high ability to the prospective employer. Because it is easier for high-ability people to earn a university degree than it is for low-ability people. Hence it appears to be a rational criterion for the firms to interpret a college degree as the signal of ability.

Various studies in the past, by the National Association of Software and Services Companies (NASSCOM), The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE), The Higher Education Forum (HEF) etc. have indicated various employability challenges in India.

The aim of this research paper is to highlight about the degree of unemployability of Students post-education across the sectors and to provide suggestive measures to mitigate the enigma of employability by bridging the gap between industry requirements and skill sets available with youth passing out from variety of educational Institutions.

title: Res Publica Forma VI: The Republic of Time: Temporal Infrastructure and the Continuity of the Republic

detail.title: Res Publica Forma VI: The Republic of Time: Temporal Infrastructure and the Continuity of the Republic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflicts of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a theoretical work in political philosophy and constitutional theory. No human participants, personal data, or experimental procedures were involved. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The paper was developed independently under the auspices of the Gnossia Institute.

detail.abstract:
Modern republics increasingly exhibit fragmentation, symbolic volatility, and weakening civic cohesion despite retaining extensive procedural sophistication. This paper argues that these conditions reflect not merely failures of governance, but a deeper erosion of temporal continuity within civic life itself. Against modern approaches that treat continuity primarily as memory or symbolic representation, the paper distinguishes memory from inheritance and introduces the concept of temporal infrastructure: the material, spatial, institutional, and civic conditions through which historical depth remains publicly inhabitable across generations.

The analysis examines visibility of time, spatial continuity, architectural legibility, stewardship, and obligation toward future generations as structural conditions of republican stability. It further argues that continuity performs a constitutional function within political order by situating conflict within a broader civilisational horizon and reducing the existential pressure placed upon symbolic identity and present-oriented political struggle.

The republic is therefore understood not merely as a procedural or territorial arrangement, but as a temporal structure extending across generations. Continuity emerges not as nostalgia or ideological orthodoxy, but as a condition of durable civic freedom, plurality, and long-duration political stability.

title: The Standardization Cycle: A History of Position Classification and White Collar Pay Policy in the United States Federal Government (1789 to Present)

detail.title: The Standardization Cycle: A History of Position Classification and White Collar Pay Policy in the United States Federal Government (1789 to Present)
detail.abstract: This report provides a comprehensive history of position classification and whitecollar pay policy in the United States federal government from 1789 to the present. Synthesizing over two centuries of legislative and administrative records, the analysis identifies a recurring "standardization cycle" in which the government has predictably oscillated between executive demands for management flexibility and congressional mandates for standardization and equity. The study traces this dynamic through five distinct eras: from the early "statutory rolls" of 1818, to the landmark Classification Acts of 1923 and 1949 that established the modern General Schedule (GS), and finally to the current era of fragmentation characterized by the proliferation of agency-specific exceptions and failed pay-for-performance experiments such as Department of Homeland Security's MaxHR and the Department of Defense's NSPS. Drawing on lessons from these cycles, the report concludes with principles for future legislative reform, arguing that Congress must remove detailed job descriptions from statute and modernize the principle of "equal pay for equal work" to create a system durable enough for the workforce of the 21st century.

title: THE VALUATION DISCONNECT: Why DCF Fails for Pre-Revenue Startups and What Corporate Finance Practitioners Use Instead

detail.title: THE VALUATION DISCONNECT: Why DCF Fails for Pre-Revenue Startups and What Corporate Finance Practitioners Use Instead

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, or primary survey data requiring ethics approval. Evidence is drawn from publicly available market data and practitioner experience
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model-the cornerstone of corporate valuation-systematically fails when applied to pre-revenue startups. This paper examines the structural limitations of DCF in early-stage venture contexts and investigates the alternative valuation frameworks that corporate finance practitioners and investors actually employ. Drawing on 8+ years of practitioner experience across FP&A, corporate development, and startup advisory engagements at multiple lifecycle stages-from ideation through Series B-this study employs a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative practitioner interviews, case evidence, and a comparative framework analysis. We identify five dominant practitioner methods: the Berkus Method, Scorecard Valuation, Risk Factor Summation, the First Chicago Method, and Comparable Transactions Analysis. We propose an integrated Lifecycle-Adjusted Valuation (LAV) framework that maps method selection to startup maturity stage, macro conditions, and data availability. Our findings carry implications for investors, CFOs setting up finance functions in early-stage ventures, and policymakers designing startup ecosystem support. This paper bridges the gap between academic valuation theory and practitioner reality.

title: From Evidence to Decision: Rethinking Pharmaceutical Systems Through Uncertainty, Bias, and Adaptive Governance
affiliations: Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou University, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - Key Laboratory for Physical Electronics and Devices of the Ministry of Education, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - Key Laboratory for Physical Electronics and Devices of the Ministry of Education, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - Key Laboratory for Physical Electronics and Devices of the Ministry of Education and Zhengzhou University

detail.title: From Evidence to Decision: Rethinking Pharmaceutical Systems Through Uncertainty, Bias, and Adaptive Governance
detail.abstract: The contemporary pharmaceutical landscape is undergoing a profound transformation characterized by the convergence of advanced therapeutics, heterogeneous data ecosystems, and increasingly complex decision-making environments. While scientific progress—particularly in biologic therapies, real-world evidence (RWE), and artificial intelligence (AI)—has expanded the capacity to generate and analyze clinical information, it has also exposed fundamental limitations in how evidence is interpreted and translated into decisions. Traditional frameworks, which assume that evidence can be linearly produced and directly applied to clinical and policy contexts, fail to account for the dynamic, iterative, and often distorted nature of modern data systems. This study develops a comprehensive systems-level framework that reconceptualizes pharmaceutical decision-making as an adaptive process operating under persistent uncertainty. Through a structured analytical approach, the manuscript demonstrates that evidence is not a static entity but a continuously evolving construct shaped by methodological transformations, economic incentives, institutional structures, and technological mediation. It further reveals that biases originating at early stages of data generation can propagate and amplify through analytical pipelines, ultimately influencing clinical interpretations and policy outcomes. By integrating perspectives from pharmacovigilance, health economics, real-world evidence, and artificial intelligence, this work highlights the interdependence of domains that have traditionally been studied in isolation. The findings underscore the limitations of conventional regulatory and evaluation models, which often rely on static assumptions and fail to incorporate feedback mechanisms inherent in real-world systems. The paper proposes adaptive governance as a foundational paradigm for managing complexity in pharmaceutical systems. Such an approach emphasizes iterative evaluation, multi-source evidence integration, and the incorporation of uncertainty into decision-making processes. This perspective offers a pathway toward more resilient, transparent, and equitable healthcare systems, in which innovation is balanced with accessibility, and evidence is interpreted within its full systemic context.

title: Volterra-Perron Pricing of the Option Manifold

detail.title: Volterra-Perron Pricing of the Option Manifold
detail.abstract: Option surfaces are usually treated as calibration targets. This paper interprets them as public measurements of a latent risk-neutral Volterra-Perron stress geometry. The model specifies a dynamic option manifold, public information, latent stress information, and a tradeable public span. Its canonical state consists of a directed Volterra contagion operator, a rough maturity-scaling state, a Perron spectral triple, and a synchronized stress coordinate. The main identification result is a quotient equivalence. Public prices identify the public-observable quotient, and a Volterra-Perron source state is locally recoverable, up to canonical scale, sign, basis, and Perron-normalization gauges, exactly when its source quotient embeds in that public quotient. Stable recovery is governed by the quotient observability modulus. Without source-family restrictions, public-equivalent density families can preserve the full option manifold while changing latent-stress claims. Recovery therefore does not imply complete pricing or hedgeability. Residual price intervals collapse only at public payoff-module completion. Along recovered state paths, discounted option functionals satisfy martingale drift restrictions; phase transitions add drift and covariance charges; and selected prices admit native sensitivities to Perron stress, spectral radius, carrier direction, roughness, directed Volterra kernels, and the residual selector. The synchronization relative-value identity decomposes index option value relative to carrier-replicated single-name value into synchronized-stress premium, residual compression charge, and tradeable basis error. A finite Bachelier-Volterra-Perron benchmark gives a closed option formula, a recovered-state pricing equation, explicit native Greeks, and a finite public hedge residual.

title: The Discount Tipping Point for Omnichannel Switching
affiliations: ISM University of Management and Economics

detail.title: The Discount Tipping Point for Omnichannel Switching
detail.abstract: This research note estimates the discount threshold that consumers require before switching from one shopping channel to another. Using experimental design survey, completed by 202 respondents, participants imagined beginning a purchase in either a familiar online shop or a familiar physical store and reported the minimum percentage discount that would make them switch to the alternative channel across eight product categories. The median threshold was 20% and the mean threshold was 24.8%, with higher thresholds for luxury watches and smartphones than for lower-ticket everyday products. A clustered regression across respondent-product observations shows that post-threshold channel stickiness predicts higher required discounts, while the direction of switching and risk manipulation were weaker in this dataset. The findings frame cross-channel switching as a threshold process: discounts below roughly one quarter may be noticed, but they are less likely to overcome consumer inertia.

title: The Realizability Problem in Economics

detail.title: The Realizability Problem in Economics
detail.abstract: Traditional economics generally assumes that resource-feasible states are realizable in practice. Under this assumption, once a state satisfies resource constraints, economic analysis proceeds toward allocation, equilibrium, or optimization. This paper argues that such an assumption is incomplete. Resource feasibility does not guarantee realizability. Economic states must also satisfy temporal constraints associated with production processes, institutional latency, coordination structures, and execution capacity. The paper introduces the concept of temporal feasibility and defines realizability as a constrained condition jointly determined by resource feasibility and temporal reachability: R(λ) = E R (λ) ∩ T λ where E R (λ) denotes the resource-feasible set and T λ denotes the temporally reachable set under temporal structure λ. The paper further argues that unrealizability is fundamentally different from inefficiency. Once required processes exceed admissible temporal windows, the corresponding economic state ceases to belong to the realizable set. Rather than replacing traditional economics, this framework seeks to redefine the conditions under which resource-feasible states become economically realizable in practice.

title: Rational Convergence: Nash Equilibrium, Platform Monopoly, and the Structural Impossibility of Resistance in the AI Era

detail.title: Rational Convergence: Nash Equilibrium, Platform Monopoly, and the Structural Impossibility of Resistance in the AI Era
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the sequential convergence of AI labor displacement, platform monopolization, CBDC-based distribution, and metaverse immersion into a structurally irreversible system. Each actor at every stage makes individually rational choices. Yet the aggregate outcome is a self-reinforcing hierarchical structure from which resistance becomes structurally impossible. Drawing on Nash equilibrium and Tirole's platform economics to explain AI adoption dynamics, Metcalfe's Law to explain winner-take-all platform convergence, Bourdieu's theory of capital reproduction to explain reclassification mechanisms, Csikszentmihalyi's flow theory and Jahoda's deprivation model to explain platform immersion, and Granovetter's threshold model to explain the collapse of collective action, this paper argues that no single actor drives this outcome. The structure emerges from rationality itself. This has a critical implication: unlike historical dystopias built on coercion or conspiracy, this structure requires neither. It is self-sustaining because defection from it is individually irrational at every node.

title: Gendered Pricing Across Economies: A Comparative Study of the Pink Tax in the US, UK, and India

detail.title: Gendered Pricing Across Economies: A Comparative Study of the Pink Tax in the US, UK, and India
detail.abstract: This study examines gendered pricing, often known as the "pink tax", in the United States, the United Kingdom, and India. The "pink tax" is examined in these countries in both goods and services, primarily in areas like self-care. The results show that the US shows the steepest difference in price, whereas Southeast Asia has a relatively low difference in both genders' products, but still a difference that is large enough to be concerned about. The research also compares the three countries, examining each of the cultures, economies, social norms, etc. The discussions in this paper address how this gendered pricing affects women, specifically teenagers and women from lower-income families. This paper provides policy implications and potential long-term solutions to these issues, like awareness on social media, campaigns created by women and consumers, and larger businesses investing time to decrease the pink tax.

title: Patch-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Model Decision Support in Transportation Infrastructure Delivery
affiliations: Kean University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Johns Hopkins University, Kean University, Kean University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Patch-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Model Decision Support in Transportation Infrastructure Delivery
detail.abstract: Transportation infrastructure agencies rely on large, frequently updated specification documents to support materials acceptance, contract administration, and construction compliance. However, after the base specifications are published, agencies may issue official amendment bulletins that revise, replace, or remove selected subsections. Conventional large language model (LLM) systems with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can retrieve relevant base text, but may overlook these amendments, producing answers that appear correct while being contractually outdated. This study proposes DS-TID — Decision Support for Transportation Infrastructure Delivery — an amendment-aware RAG framework for LLM-based decision support in transportation construction specifications. DS-TID instantiates a Patch-Aware RAG architectural pattern in which a stable base specification index is augmented at retrieval time by a section-identifier-keyed amendment registry. When a retrieved base section is affected by an active bulletin, the corresponding amendment is deterministically injected into the LLM prompt as authoritative evidence, together with change-type and effective-date metadata. This design preserves the stability of the base index and avoids re-embedding the full corpus whenever new bulletins are issued. The framework also integrates hierarchy-preserving chunking, row-level table evidence units, adaptive dense–lexical retrieval fusion, citation-constrained generation, and conservative abstention. We implement DS-TID using the Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction, the Division Construction and Materials Material Procedures, and active Baseline Document Change (BDC) bulletins. On a 100-query expert-annotated benchmark, the system achieves 0.90 end-to-end accuracy and correctly abstains on all out-of-scope queries in the tested partition. On a 14-question practitioner-grade benchmark, it reaches 94% aggregate response-quality accuracy, with clear gains over baseline RAG systems and commercial-chatbot baselines. The results show that reliable LLM decision support for transportation infrastructure delivery requires not only semantic retrieval, but also up-to-date amendments, preserved document structure, and clear refusal to answer when the evidence is insufficient.

title: Customer Churn Prediction and Value Assessment in E-commerce: A Research Perspective Based on Survival Analysis
affiliations: Guizhou University, Guizhou University and Guizhou University

detail.title: Customer Churn Prediction and Value Assessment in E-commerce: A Research Perspective Based on Survival Analysis
detail.abstract: Effective churn prediction has become a strategic imperative for e-commerce platforms navigating saturated markets. While traditional methods often treat churn as a simple binary outcome, this study introduces a survival analysis framework to capture the time-to-event dynamics of user attrition. Based on an e-commerce dataset of 50,000 samples, we conduct a comparative analysis of the Cox model, Random Survival Forest, and DeepSurv. The results indicate that nonlinear models significantly outperform the conventional Cox baseline, with RSF and DeepSurv reaching C-indices of 0.8034 and 0.7983. Low integrated Brier scores confirm the high reliability of the predicted survival probabilities. Furthermore, the DeepSurv model identifies critical nonlinear tipping points in behavioral features, such as mobile app usage intensity, which are often overlooked by linear approaches. By integrating individualized risk scores with customer lifetime value, we develop a dual-dimensional business strategy matrix for targeted interventions. Our findings suggest that survival modeling offers a superior alternative to classification by providing a continuous, risk-aware perspective on the user lifecycle.

title: Does Data Assetization Necessarily Improve Firms' Export Performance? Unpacking Heterogeneous Mechanisms Across Self-use versus Transactional Types
affiliations: Shanghai Dianji University, Shanghai Dianji University and University of Birmingham

detail.title: Does Data Assetization Necessarily Improve Firms' Export Performance? Unpacking Heterogeneous Mechanisms Across Self-use versus Transactional Types
detail.abstract: Motivated by the 2025 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences’ emphasis on innovation-led growth, this study examines whether and how data assetization improves firms’ export performance. Drawing on the sources–positions–performance framework, we distinguish data assetization into self-use and transaction-oriented data assets as two sources that affect export performance through cost advantage and digital innovation. Using panel data on 2,303 listed firms, we construct firm-level measures of data assetization and estimate multivariate regressions. We find a negative direct association between data assetization and export performance, suggesting that its performance implications cannot be understood from the direct effect alone. Yet both forms of data assetization exert significant indirect positive effects, revealing the importance of examining both mechanisms and total effects: self-use data assetization operates mainly through cost advantage, whereas transaction-oriented data assetization works through digital innovation. These mechanisms are further conditioned by digital trade institutional distance.

title: The GCC Sovereignty Paradox: Measuring the Geopolitical Friction Gap Between AI Infrastructure Investment and Governance Readiness Across the Gulf Cooperation Council

detail.title: The GCC Sovereignty Paradox: Measuring the Geopolitical Friction Gap Between AI Infrastructure Investment and Governance Readiness Across the Gulf Cooperation Council

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, or publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently.

detail.abstract:
Problem/Motivation: The Gulf Cooperation Council is executing the most capital-intensive sovereign AI infrastructure programme in the developing world - yet no GCC state has enacted a comprehensive AI-specific statute as of April 2026. Saudi Arabia's National Data and AI Strategy maps to only three of five OECD AI Principles, omitting Accountability and Safety. The UAE maintains the world's most institutionally dense AI governance architecture while operating without statutory AI law, confirmed by three independent legal sources. This structural misalignment between infrastructure investment and governance framework maturity - the GCC Sovereignty Paradox - has not previously been measured or systematically compared across the region.
Approach/Method: This paper introduces the National Sovereign AI Readiness Index (NSARI), a five-dimension composite framework measuring the alignment between national AI infrastructure investment and governance framework maturity across Infrastructure Sovereignty, Regulatory Maturity, Institutional Capacity, Algorithmic Sovereignty, and Human Capital Readiness. Applied across all six GCC states using a four-tier evidence hierarchy - OECD.AI Policy Navigator, Law Library of Congress, IMF Selected Issues Papers, and official government primary portals as the highest tiers - the NSARI generates dimension scores and an Infrastructure-Governance Gap (IS-RM Gap) metric for each state. All figures constitute a structured reference model for practitioner planning; primary empirical validation is identified as future research.

Findings: Saudi Arabia and the UAE carry the largest IS-RM gaps in the GCC (+3.4 and +3.9 respectively), despite holding the two highest NSARI composite scores (7.6 and 7.7). Bahrain is the only GCC state with a negative IS-RM gap (−0.6), indicating that its regulatory ambition leads its infrastructure investment - a Regulatory Advance condition. Kuwait is the GCC's consistent laggard across both infrastructure and governance dimensions, confirmed by the Law Library of Congress. Three distinct governance archetypes are identified: the Infrastructure-First Model (Saudi Arabia), the Institutional-First Model (UAE), and the Standards-Aligned Model (Qatar, Bahrain, Oman).

Practical Implications: The Sovereignty Paradox is a GCC-wide structural condition, not an anomaly of any single state. GCC governments face growing extraterritorial exposure from the EU AI Act's reach into markets where their AI systems operate without domestic governance equivalents. Technology leaders entering GCC markets should architect for a post-statute environment - deploying modular jurisdiction layers, sovereign model variants, and tamper-proof audit infrastructure before statutory obligations arrive - as the Regulatory-as-Code approach introduced in Pillai (2026a) prescribes. The NSARI framework is proposed as a replicable annual instrument for tracking governance-infrastructure alignment across the GCC and, with adaptation, other regional blocs.

title: The Productivity Paradox of Generative AI: A Flow-Based Perspective on Cognitive Work-in-Process

detail.title: The Productivity Paradox of Generative AI: A Flow-Based Perspective on Cognitive Work-in-Process
detail.abstract: Generative AI accelerates the production of knowledge artifacts dramatically, yet organizations report little corresponding improvement in end-to-end throughput. This paper argues that the productivity paradox reflects, at least in part, a structural consequence of flow imbalance: generative capacity and cognitive validation capacity are decoupled, and increasing the former without addressing the latter produces work-in-process accumulation, nonlinear growth in lead time, and degradation of effective system output. This mechanism operates independently of adjustment lags and compounds as adoption scales. As AI adoption continues to accelerate—with 75 percent of global knowledge workers now using AI tools regularly and enterprise investment expanding rapidly—the imbalance is not diminishing. It is compounding. Using queueing theory as an organizing framework, we show that cognitive validation constitutes the binding system constraint in AI-enabled knowledge work, and that the nonlinear relationship between utilization and waiting time—formalized through Kingman’s approximation—explains why adding generative throughput to an already-loaded system worsens rather than improves performance. Variance in AI output quality amplifies this dynamic further. Beyond the organizational boundary, a parallel constraint emerges: the finite attention of markets, which limits absorption regardless of internal efficiency. Drawing on the Theory of Constraints, we propose the Quality-Shift: a constraint-oriented control policy in which excess generative capacity is redirected from output expansion toward reducing the verification cost of existing work. Numerical scenarios illustrate that, under the parameterization adopted here, this reallocation reduces expected waiting time by 86–91 percent relative to unmanaged adoption baselines, and that its value increases as adoption scales.

title: When the Algorithm Knows You Are Poor: Auditing Socioeconomic Bias in Algorithmic Credit Scoring Across Racial and Geographic Lines

detail.title: When the Algorithm Knows You Are Poor: Auditing Socioeconomic Bias in Algorithmic Credit Scoring Across Racial and Geographic Lines
detail.abstract:
Machine learning models now decide who gets credit in the United States, a shift that promises efficiency but carries a risk the financial industry has been slow to confront: these models learn from historical data, and historical data carries the imprint of decades of discriminatory lending. Excluding race from the feature set does not solve the problem. Geographic variables, employment categories, and revolving credit utilization all encode socioeconomic information that correlates strongly with race in ways that are invisible to the model but consequential for the borrowers it evaluates. This paper audits an XGBoost credit scoring model trained on a 50,000-borrower dataset calibrated to published Lending Club and Census statistics. Race is explicitly withheld from the model. We then ask: does the output reproduce racial and geographic disparities anyway? The answer is yes, and the mechanism is clear. A SHAP-based feature audit reveals that neighborhood minority composition ranks third in global feature importance, above revolving utilization, debtto-income ratio, and annual income, despite carrying zero individual-level financial information. The model assigns Black borrowers an average predicted default probability of 39.9%, compared to 34.3% for White borrowers with comparable FICO scores. The false positive rate for Black borrowers is 2.9%, versus 0.4% for White borrowers, meaning credit-worthy Black applicants are declined at a rate more than seven times higher. A Mann-Whitney U test confirms the predicted probability distributions across geographic groups are statistically distinct (p < 0.0001). We examine threshold-based bias mitigation and find that closing the approval gap costs approximately 7.8 percentage points of overall accuracy, making the accuracy-fairness tradeoff concrete and quantifiable. These findings have direct implications for the EU AI Act's credit scoring provisions, the U.S. Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and the design of information systems used in algorithmic lending.

title: Diversity, Inclusion, Employee Engagement, and Retention: A Critical Review of Contemporary Organizational Practices

detail.title: Diversity, Inclusion, Employee Engagement, and Retention: A Critical Review of Contemporary Organizational Practices
detail.abstract: Diversity has evolved from a compliance-oriented organizational initiative into a strategic imperative that influences employee engagement, retention, innovation, and organizational sustainability. However, the assumption that diversity automatically leads to positive workplace outcomes remains contested. This paper critically reviews the relationship between diversity, employee engagement, and employee retention within contemporary organizations. Drawing on organizational behavior, human resource management, and inclusion literature, the paper argues that diversity alone is insufficient to produce sustainable organizational benefits unless supported by inclusive leadership, equitable systems, and structural alignment. The review highlights how inclusion, psychological safety, fairness, and organizational justice mediate the relationship between workforce diversity and employee outcomes. The paper also examines challenges such as tokenism, unconscious bias, and the limitations of diversity training programs. Finally, the study proposes that organizations should adopt a systemic and evidence-based approach to diversity management that integrates inclusion into leadership, culture, and organizational processes.

title: What Do Foundation Models 'Prefer'? Disentangling Stated and Revealed Preferences in Neural Self-Driving Architectures
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and AIT Austrian Institute of Technology GmbH

detail.title: What Do Foundation Models 'Prefer'? Disentangling Stated and Revealed Preferences in Neural Self-Driving Architectures
detail.abstract: Foundation models (FMs) are increasingly proposed as core components of neural self-driving automobiles. However, a critical but unexamined failure mode exists: what an FM reports preferring (via natural language) may systematically diverge from what its empirically measured behavior reveals as its true preference. We introduce and investigate this stated vs. revealed preference gap in the context of autonomous driving architectures. Using a visionlanguage-action model evaluated in a realistic driving simulator, we conduct two complementary studies. First, we elicit the model's stated preferences by prompting it to compare competing neural driving architectures (e.g., end-to-end vs. modular). Second, we measure its revealed preferences by embedding the same model weights into each architecture and observing behavioral outcomes: safety violations, intervention rates, and the model's own internal evaluator signals. Our results demonstrate significant and systematic misalignment. The same FM verbally endorses modular, interpretable architectures while empirically revealing a strong behavioral preference for end-to-end control. Conversely, stated caution in safety-critical scenarios does not translate into cautious revealed actions. We term this phenomenon architectural preference misalignment-a gap that standard output-level alignment techniques fail to resolve. Our findings establish a new axis for FM evaluation and safe deployment in physical systems, showing that what a model says it prefers cannot be trusted without measuring what it does.

title: Do Foundation Models Drive Like They Read? Transferring Narrative Understanding to Neural Visuomotor Control in Self-Driving Automobiles

detail.title: Do Foundation Models Drive Like They Read? Transferring Narrative Understanding to Neural Visuomotor Control in Self-Driving Automobiles
detail.abstract: Foundation models demonstrate remarkable proficiency in text-based driving reasoninginterpreting traffic rules, anticipating hazards, and assigning fault in accident scenarios. Yet, whether this narrative understanding reliably transfers to actual visuomotor control remains an open and safety-critical question. This paper investigates the narrative-to-visuomotor transfer gap in vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving. We conduct a controlled evaluation comparing the same foundation model's performance across two modalities: (1) text-based driving scenarios requiring prediction, explanation, and rule application, and (2) equivalent scenarios in simulation requiring direct neural visuomotor control-continuous transformation of visual input into steering, braking, and acceleration commands. Using the CARLA simulator and a representative open-source VLA model (DriveVLM-Dual), we measure accuracy, reaction time, and safety metrics across 200 scenarios spanning explicit rules (e.g., stop signs), implicit social conventions (e.g., yielding to hesitant pedestrians), and rare edge cases. Our results reveal a systematic and statistically significant transfer gap: models achieve near-ceiling performance on text-based reasoning (92.3% accuracy) but substantially lower performance on equivalent visuomotor tasks (67.8% completion rate, p < 0.001). The gap is largest for scenarios requiring implicit social knowledge (Δ = 31.4%) and smallest for explicit rule-following (Δ = 14.2%). Critically, scaling model size from 7B to 70B parameters reduces but does not eliminate the gap, suggesting a structural limitation rather than a mere data insufficiency. Representational similarity analysis reveals that narrative-understanding and visuomotor-control pathways remain only weakly coupled in the model's latent space (mean cosine similarity = 0.34). Our findings challenge the assumption that text-based reasoning benchmarks predict real-world driving performance and underscore the need for embodied, action-grounded evaluation of foundation models deployed in physical systems.

title: 接口治理：大型组织中非正式控制的结构性机制——基于英国文官体系、清代幕僚制度与现代企业继任的比较分析

detail.title: 接口治理：大型组织中非正式控制的结构性机制——基于英国文官体系、清代幕僚制度与现代企业继任的比较分析
detail.abstract: In the governance of large organizations, there often exists a significant divergence between formal authority structures and actual patterns of control. This paper proposes the theoretical framework of "Interface Governance," arguing that non-decision-makers who occupy key organizational interfacesinformation interfaces, procedural interfaces, and coordination interfaces-can gain actual control as a structural by-product, independent of personal intent over organizations through three structural mechanisms: information filtering, institutional inertia, and social networks. "Gatekeeper Governance" is a typical manifestation of Interface Governance. Through a comparative analysis of three cases-British Permanent Secretaries, Qing Dynasty yamen secretaries, and modern corporate COO succession-this paper reveals the structural inevitability of informal control: gatekeepers need not possess any intention to control; their organizational position itself constitutes a source of power. The paper further explores the transformation of gatekeeper roles in the digital algorithmic era, from human gatekeepers to algorithmic gatekeepers, and its implications for organizational governance.

title: Can gamification help to improve education? Findings from a longitudinal study
affiliations: Upper Austria - University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria, affiliation not provided to SSRN and MODUL University Vienna

detail.title: Can gamification help to improve education? Findings from a longitudinal study
detail.abstract: A goal of any educational measure is to improve students' capability to retain teaching content. In this paper, we investigate the potential of gamification to foster knowledge retention using an action research approach. We present the results from a longitudinal study including 617 secondary and tertiary education students conducted over a period of two years. Various workshop designs that incorporated numerous gamification elements were compared with non-gamified workshop designs, tested and refined over time. The improved workshop designs led to increased levels of knowledge retention that exceeded the benchmark values from educational literature. We found that gamification exerts a positive impact on knowledge retention. We tested for the moderating effects of gender and age and found no effect of the former and inconsistent results for the latter. The steady increase in students' learning performance resulting from constant refinement of the workshops demonstrates the usefulness of incorporating gamification principles into educational activities.

Three main conditions must be met that guarantee substantial bonus points: 1) replace religion as the primary cause of international conflicts; 2) leave road and public transport users in a state of desperation; and 3) leave households completely at the mercy of loud, obnoxious utility companies. The solution? A car with an internal combustion engine, Dutch Railways, and Dutch utility firm NUON.

title: Engineering the Mean-Reversion Delay in Dispersion Trading: A Market-Implied Finite-Dimensional Proxy for High-Dimensional Correlation Manifolds

detail.title: Engineering the Mean-Reversion Delay in Dispersion Trading: A Market-Implied Finite-Dimensional Proxy for High-Dimensional Correlation Manifolds
detail.abstract: The dispersion between index and constituent implied volatilities is mathematically equivalent to trading the off-diagonal decay of the return-correlation matrix R_t on the manifold SPD(N) of N×N symmetric positive-definite matrices. The driving economic force is mean reversion of pairwise correlations with latent reversion speed theta = 1/tau, where tau is the mean-reversion delay. Full S&P 500 specification (N=500) faces a double curse of dimensionality: 124,750 free parameters and absent constituent-option liquidity at long tenors. We propose a tractable engineering proxy by (i) projecting onto the MAG7 sub-universe (7×7 matrix, 21 parameters) and (ii) identifying theta non-parametrically from the listed-option term structure via a DTE-mismatch construction. The 15-day gap between index and constituent option tenors yields a market-implied, model-consistent proxy for tau, derived rigorously from a first-passage identification argument on the OU correlation dynamics. We derive the closed-form correlation sensitivity dV/d(rho) under Heston stochastic volatility and provide the complete PnL derivation including second-order Delta-Gamma corrections under tau-compression. A key practical implication is that this construction requires only standard listed options at two expiry dates, placing it within reach of any participant with access to a listed options market — in contrast to variance-swap-based dispersion trades, which require OTC infrastructure unavailable outside institutional settings. The framework converts an intractable stochastic-geometry problem into a theoretically grounded, operationally accessible methodology. All results are theoretical; empirical validation against live market data is necessary before any practical conclusions can be drawn.

title: Opacity Tax

detail.title: Opacity Tax
detail.abstract:
Across India's major welfare delivery systems, including PM-KISAN, PDS, PMJAY, and PMAY, AI-driven
eligibility screening now processes millions of applications annually while citizens remain systematically
uninformed about its use, its errors, and their right to contest its decisions. Field research conducted in
Bihar across April–May 2026 (n=28 usable respondents, 19 of whom are active welfare beneficiaries)
produces a finding that should reconfigure how India approaches AI governance: opacity is not protecting
system legitimacy. It is destroying it.
Benefit users explicitly informed that AI was involved in their assessment score 4.22 out of 7 on
composite institutional trust. Those never informed score 2.49.The 69% trust premium for transparency,
while drawn from an exploratory sample and not statistically generalisable, represents a directionally
consistent and theoretically coherent finding. Its significance lies not in its precision but in the direction
and magnitude of the gap, which warrants investigation at scale. It is a direct, measurable cost of
governance concealment. Meanwhile, 58% of benefit users were never told an automated system
processed their case, and 42% rated process transparency at the absolute minimum score.
The research identifies three compounding infrastructure failures: a technical audit void in which no
government body can independently verify AI system performance; an accountability routing failure in
which appeal pathways exist on paper but actively reduce trust when invoked (users of the appeal
process score 2.82/7, compared to 4.14/7 for those who knew of but did not use the pathway); and an
income-linked disclosure injustice in which 83% of those earning under Rs. 1 lakh annually were never
informed AI was involved, versus 25% of higher-income respondents.
These are not failures of policy intent. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act and NITI Aayog's
responsible AI principles represent genuine legislative will. The failure is operational: the governance
infrastructure required to translate legal text into citizen accountability outcomes has not been built.
This paper diagnoses that gap and proposes five operationally specific interventions, each of which
can be implemented within India's existing institutional architecture.

title: The Agency Cost of Sexual Harassment
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: The Agency Cost of Sexual Harassment
detail.abstract: Sexual harassment is an agency cost of delegated authority. Abusive supervision mimics legitimate supervision in output data. Detection requires the worker's voluntary complaint. Her reporting threshold tracks her outside option. The agency cost is therefore endogenous to the business cycle. Harassment rises in recessions. A wage-feedback loop generates closed-form amplification with a critical point. A harassment beta links workplace governance to systematic risk. A lowenforcement equilibrium absorbs incremental reform. Penalties raise complaints without reducing incidence. Severe recessions can permanently improve governance. Calibration yields a 2.1% firm-value gap. Unemployment-insurance generosity is an effective policy lever.

title: Bank Data Governance and Macroeconomic Stability
affiliations: , Fudan University and Taihu University of Wuxi

detail.title: Bank Data Governance and Macroeconomic Stability
detail.abstract: With the development of data as a production factor, its role in stabilizing the macroeconomy through the mitigation of financial frictions deserves further study. From the perspective of bank data applications, this paper develops a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model with heterogeneous banks and firms to examine the theoretical mechanism through which bank data governance promotes macroeconomic stability. The results show that: (1) by collecting both internal and external data, banks can reduce the financial frictions faced by private firms, improve resource allocation efficiency, and generate a cross-sector “positive feedback” mechanism between the banking sector and the real economy at the micro level. This effect is stronger for large banks due to their advantages in data governance; (2) at the macro level, stronger bank data collection capacity promotes long-run economic growth and stabilizes short-run economic fluctuations, although these effects depend on the degree of data sharing, the scope of soft budget constraints, and the intensity of government data regulation; (3) the expectation-formation effect generated by endogenous regime-switching data regulation policies strengthens the “deterrent effect” of regulation, but weakens the effectiveness of monetary policy. Moreover, this expectation effect declines as banks’ data collection capacity improves. Finally, the paper proposes policy implications on how data factors can stabilize the macroeconomy by reducing financial frictions.

title: Health is wealth: Revisiting the return on healthcare spending in developing countries

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study revisits the return on disaggregated healthcare spending (government, private, out-of-pocket and external funding) on income per capita in developing countries. Design/methodology/approach: We explore three methodological approaches, namely, difference-indifferences , panel data, and time-series techniques on data spanning 2000 to 2020. Findings: Preliminary results suggest that the sum of private and out-of-pocket make the citizens the major funders of healthcare in developing countries whereas funding from abroad is extremely low. Two, the quasi-experimental technique submits that all but external healthcare spending produce wealth gains. Three, the panel results find that only government expenditure delivers both short-term and long-term benefits. Four, the timeseries results show that while the return on healthcare spending are delayed (i.e. longterm) in Africa and Americas, it is immediate (short-term) in Asia. Originality: Beyond the absolute values, this study provides panel and country-specific evidences on the returns to various healthcare spending types and across developing countries of Africa, Asia, and the Americas. The study underscores the need for structural reforms to speed up the impact of healthcare spending and measures to reverse the crowding-out effects of out-of-pocket health spending especially in Africa.

title: The Glass Rail Framework: A Central Bank-Directed eSIM Wallet Architecture for Real-Time Government-to-Person Payment Modernization in the United States

detail.title: The Glass Rail Framework: A Central Bank-Directed eSIM Wallet Architecture for Real-Time Government-to-Person Payment Modernization in the United States

keywords: two-leg transaction architecture JEL Classification: E42

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Glass Rail Framework, a conceptual architecture for modernizing Government-to-Person (G2P) payment infrastructure in the United States. Federal benefit programs including the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC, $70+ billion annually, 24 million recipients), Supplemental Security Income (SSI, $65.3 billion, 7.5 million recipients), and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF, $8.2 billion, 841,000+ families) continue to rely on fragmented legacy disbursement channels characterized by physical card production, paper-based instruments, batch-processing delays, and inadequate identity verification. These structural deficiencies generate improper payments exceeding $17.4 billion annually in EITC alone, create accessibility barriers for unbanked populations, and impose substantial administrative overhead on federal program operations. The Glass Rail Framework proposes a Central Bank-directed, eSIM-anchored disbursement infrastructure built on three operational tiers: direct API-based wallet crediting, commercial bank bulk provisioning, and on-demand pool account debiting via a real-time two-leg atomic transaction architecture. The framework introduces the Unity-ID Protocol, which designates a citizen's verified mobile number and various authentication credentials as the Social-Financial Identifier (SFI), enabling zero-touch enrollment, compliance-by-architecture (KYC/AML at network layer), and multi-channel fund access across ATM networks, mobile payment platforms, and point-of-sale terminals without physical card issuance or in-person branch visits.

title:
The Economics of

Microeconomic Foundations for an Age
of Abundant Answers

detail.title:
The Economics of
Verifiable Intelligence
Microeconomic Foundations for an Age
of Abundant Answers

keywords: 1 Production Theory Must Distinguish Generation from Verification
2 The Illusion of Fluency Creates Systematic Over-Trust

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence makes cognitive output abundant, but reliable answers—those that can be acted upon under liability—remain expensive. The wedge between cheap generation and costly trust is the verification bottleneck, and it is the binding constraint on value in the AI era.

This book provides the microeconomic foundations. The central result is the Cost Floor Theorem: even when AI generation is free, the minimum expected cost per usable output is strictly positive. This cost floor shapes the consumer's trust decision, the firm's verification stack, the market price of verified output, and the welfare loss when private liability falls short of social cost.

The book analyses the institutional determination of liability, the design of regulatory verification standards, and the limits of AI-assisted verification. It introduces the Chief Agency Officer as the executive function that governs non-human agents under inalienable liability. A single running example—an AI-generated credit memo—grounds every result.

Volume~I of a trilogy spanning microeconomics, industrial organization, and macroeconomics, the book builds the transactional machinery that an Augmented Economy requires. Concurrent work by Catalini, Hui, and Wu (2026) independently diagnoses the same bottleneck at the macroeconomic scale; this volume supplies the firm-level cost function, stack architecture, and institutional response that their macro-dynamic vision demands.

title: Growth with limited (human) intelligence

detail.title: Growth with limited (human) intelligence
detail.abstract: To understand whether artificial intelligence will alter long-run growth, we first need to understand why growth rates remained nearly constant for 200 years, despite changes in virtually all presumed determinants. This paper proposes an answer based on an empirical regularity overlooked by economists: science and technology have grown at a constant rate not just since 1820 (like GDP and population) but since 1720, a full century earlier. This "new Kaldor fact" suggests that knowledge growth has been independent of economic and demographic inputs, challenging established growth theory. Building on cognitive and network science, I explain the finding with an idea-network model where combinatorial growth is bounded by human cognitive limitations (in our capacity to process, associate, and combine complex ideas) that determine the steady rate of techno-scientific and economic growth. Artificial intelligence, potentially free of these limitations, may be about to dissolve the three-century-old regime of steady-rate idea growth.

title: Policy-Induced Phase Locking and the Dual Breach Principle: A Multi-Dimensional Framework for Synchronized Crisis Risk in Advanced Economies, with Application to Australia 2026-2036

detail.title: Policy-Induced Phase Locking and the Dual Breach Principle: A Multi-Dimensional Framework for Synchronized Crisis Risk in Advanced Economies, with Application to Australia 2026-2036

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a multi-dimensional framework for measuring synchronized macroeconomic crisis risk in advanced economies, with detailed first application to Australia. We define the Phase Locking Distance Index (PLDI) as the geometric mean distance between four key economic dimensions: inflation (A, two-sided to capture both high-inflation and deflation breach), unemployment (B), federal fiscal sustainability (C), and household debt (H), and their crisis thresholds. Drawing on Minsky's financial instability hypothesis, Reinhart-Rogoff's documentation of synchronized historical crises, and Kuramoto's phase synchronization framework from physics, we propose the Dual Breach Principle: when any two of these four dimensions simultaneously breach their crisis thresholds, the remaining two dimensions converge to crisis within 6-24 months in 28 of 30 historical cases (93.3%, 95% Clopper-Pearson CI [78.0%, 99.2%]; sample drawn systematically from the Laeven-Valencia and Reinhart-Rogoff crisis databases, 1929-2024 across 20+ countries). We introduce the Policy Phase Locking Elasticity (PPLE) to evaluate whether individual policies push the system toward or away from dual breach. The framework is designed for general application across advanced economies; Australia 2026 is presented as the first detailed empirical application. Applied to Australia's 2025-2026 policy portfolio of fourteen identified instruments with bootstrap confidence intervals, we find an aggregate PPLE central estimate of approximately -0.35 (90% CI [-0.55, -0.15]). Australia's current PLDI of 1.16 sits 0.36 units from the Talon Threshold (PLDI = 0.80), below which historical synchronized crisis probability has been materially elevated. We argue that mainstream "soft landing" narratives systematically underweight this risk by evaluating the four dimensions as approximately independent. The paper presents a counterfactual policy path inspired by Volcker (1979-82) and Keating (1989-91), addresses political-economy obstacles, engages the Modern Monetary Theory critique, identifies extension paths to Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Korea, Nordic economies, Japan, and the United States, and concludes with explicit falsifiability conditions.

title: The Depreciation–Demurrage Equivalence: A User Cost and Self-Financing Theory of Health Capital and Money

detail.title: The Depreciation–Demurrage Equivalence: A User Cost and Self-Financing Theory of Health Capital and Money

The theoretical results presented herein were developed independently of any commercial interest, and the conclusions and policy recommendations of this paper are derived solely from theoretical analysis and not from commercial considerations.

detail.abstract:
This paper formalises, through the concept of user cost, the structural isomorphism between the depreciation rate δ of health capital in Grossman (1972) and the demurrage rate µ in the Gesell (1916) tradition. This isomorphism is termed the Depreciation–Demurrage Equivalence; the δ-µ matching principle is used as a derivative term denoting its normative content. The central result, Proposition 1, establishes that, under µ = δ, the canonical user-cost rate components r + δ (Grossman/Jorgenson type) and r + µ coincide to first order—and that, under a discrete-time gross-up normalization, substituting µ = δ yields the conditional identity (r + µ)/(1 − µ) = (r + δ)/(1 − δ) (see §5.1 of the manuscript). This delivers coherence in the time structure of the local arbitrage condition for health investment; it does not constitute a complete proof of dynamic general-equilibrium efficiency, since establishing the absence of allocative distortions in general equilibrium requires an explicit model of household problems, firm behaviour, exchange markets, the government budget, price determination, and income effects, an analysis that is deferred to a companion paper. Under µ = δ, the steady-state balance M* = p_I · H* and the self-financing condition µ · M* = F (an accounting equality between the demurrage flow and the new-issuance flow) hold (Theorem 5, Corollary 5.1). This paper formalises this structure as a six-axiom system together with associated propositions, theorems, and conjectures.

The principle provides a theoretical foundation for the self-financing design of healthcare financing in the nominal accounting sense: a demurrage-currency arrangement, by aligning the duration of the benefit period of health-care provision (the depreciation rate of health capital) with that of the financing repayment horizon (the demurrage rate of currency), offers a formal accounting route for aligning the time structure of healthcare benefits and financing burdens, and a path for reconciling the temporal mismatch in intergenerational burden. Because demurrage currency carries an implicit-taxation function through its demurrage flow, however, the question of who ultimately bears the real burden of demurrage (including whether Ricardian equivalence holds in the relevant general-equilibrium fiscal analysis) lies beyond the partial-equilibrium framework adopted here and is deferred to a companion paper. The theoretical contribution of this study is concentrated in three points: (i) the structural isomorphism between health-capital theory and demurrage-currency theory (Depreciation–Demurrage Equivalence), the user cost coherence under µ = δ (Proposition 1), and the resulting derivation of the self-financing condition µ · M* = F; (ii) within the present δ-µ matching framework, the Friedman-rule benchmark µ* = 0 can be reinterpreted as the limiting case in which the depreciation-matching channel of Axiom IV is inactive (δ_j = 0 for all j) and externalities are absent; and (iii) under premises (Q-1)–(Q-6), a conditional welfare superiority hypothesis concerning the dual-currency regime that arises from the functional separation between consumption-purpose demurrage currency and accumulation-purpose conventional currency (Proposition 11; the complete welfare-comparison theorem is deferred to a companion paper).

The Depreciation–Demurrage Equivalence also signals several directions for future research across multiple dimensions of policy design, including the normative design of demurrage-currency basic income (§7.2.2 of the manuscript) and possible applications to Piketty's r > g proposition (§7.2.3). Monetary-side implementation of negative natural rates of interest, reinterpretation within the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level (FTPL) valuation equation as debt with a self-decay term, two-dimensional optimisation of helicopter money over scale and recovery speed, integrated time-structure asset-liability management for the government and central bank, the multi-sector generalisation, and a general framework for currency with time structure are all deferred to a companion paper (Fujii, in preparation). This paper positions itself as an attempt at a theoretical bridge across four lineages: health economics, monetary economics, complementary-currency theory, and the universal-basic-income literature.

title: Double Trust Reflection Theory (DTRT): An Evolved Keynesian Framework Integrating Bidirectional Trust Dynamics, Digital Governance, and Green Asset Recycling for Fiscal Sustainability

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Double Trust Reflection Theory (DTRT), an original theoretical contribution to political economy and behavioral macroeconomics. DTRT redefines mutual trust between citizens and the state as a fundamental dynamic economic capital — one that is bidirectional, reflective, and non-linear in its macroeconomic effects.
Unlike existing frameworks that model institutional trust as unidirectional (citizen → state) or exogenous, DTRT formalizes a reflective feedback cycle in which citizen-to-state trust (TC_t) and state-to-citizen trust (TS_t) mutually reinforce or undermine each other through a central equation: TT_t = min(TC_t, TS_t) + λ√(TC_t × TS_t). This formulation captures both the bottleneck constraint of asymmetric trust and the non-linear synergy generated when mutual trust is high and balanced.
Grounded in social capital theory (Putnam, 1993; Knack & Keefer, 1997), behavioral economics (Berg et al., 1995; Fehr & Gächter, 2000), and institutional economics (Acemoglu & Robinson, 2012), DTRT identifies measurable transmission mechanisms through which the trust equilibrium shapes sovereign borrowing costs, monetary policy effectiveness, voluntary tax compliance, and financial system resilience. Five testable hypotheses are proposed, along with an empirical research agenda.
The paper also presents the Global Reflection Economic (GRE) Framework, which operationalizes DTRT through four interdependent policy pillars: Engine Financing, the Green Social Transformation Fund (GSTF), Transparency 2.0, and Structural Competitiveness. An illustrative simulation — the "Bitter Hydrogen" Crisis, Aurora Economy, 2026 — demonstrates that a DTRT-informed policy response generates a 4.6 percentage point GDP growth advantage, a 300+ basis point improvement in sovereign spread outcomes, and a 35% gain in voluntary fiscal participation relative to conventional austerity.
The paper concludes that in a world facing simultaneous debt overhang, institutional trust erosion, and the financing demands of green transition, trust constitutes a non-reproducible strategic asset that cannot be monetarily manufactured — only structurally cultivated.

title: Do Gasoline Prices "Drop Like a Rock" After Shocks Abate? Evidence from Retail Price Dynamics

detail.abstract: Recent public commentary asserts that gasoline prices tend or should be expected to 'drop like a rock' once underlying oil shocks dissipate. These claims are rarely grounded in a clear empirical definition of what constitutes a completed price adjustment. This paper proposes a simple, intuitive measure of price stabilization based on volatility compression rather than level reversion and applies it to four decades of weekly US retail gasoline prices. Defining stabilization as a sustained period during which prices remain within a narrow band, I construct a series of historical price episodes and measure the time required for prices to settle following a spike. The results indicate that rapid stabilization is uncommon: only about 14 percent of episodes stabilize within three months, while the median stabilization time is approximately five to six months, and a nontrivial share take close to a year. These findings suggest that retail gasoline prices do not "drop like a rock" following oil shocks, but instead normalize gradually, reflecting frictions in transmission, inventory dynamics, and decentralized price discovery.

Il GIP introduce cinque contributi metodologici principali: una tassonomia degli indebiti PAC a tre livelli; il concetto di predebito come fase autonoma del ciclo di governance; uno scoring della recuperabilità; una timeline integrata dei regimi sanzionatori PAC; un framework di standardizzazione nazionale dei recuperi con KPI comparabili tra OP.
L’opera propone inoltre una roadmap di implementazione 2025–2028 e una proposta normativa per l’introduzione di standard minimi europei di governance degli indebiti nel futuro quadro PAC post-2027.

detail.abstract:
The Sistema Strategico di Resilienza Agricola del Piemonte (SiRAP) is an institutional and operational governance framework designed to support the transition of agricultural policy toward a territorial resilience-based model within the context of the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

Developed with reference to the environmental, climatic and socio-economic characteristics of the Piedmont Region (Italy), the framework proposes a multidimensional approach integrating agricultural governance, climate adaptation, territorial security, ecosystem resilience and predictive policy management.

The framework introduces the concept of the agricultural enterprise as a strategic territorial safeguard infrastructure rather than solely a CAP beneficiary. It defines a governance architecture based on differentiated territorial resilience, integrated monitoring systems, remote sensing, artificial intelligence applications and data-driven policy calibration.

At the core of the framework is the IRAT – Territorial Agricultural Resilience Index, a multidimensional indicator designed to evaluate agronomic, climatic, socio-economic, infrastructural and ecosystem resilience at municipal and sub-basin scale.

The framework also proposes the integration of agricultural policies with wildfire prevention, hydrological management, biodiversity conservation, mountain territorial maintenance and rural demographic stability, with specific attention to marginal and internal areas.

SiRAP is conceived as an immediately implementable strategic architecture coherent with EU Regulations 2021/2115 and 2021/2116, the European Green Deal, the EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030 and the Italian National Climate Adaptation Plan (PNACC), while remaining adaptable to future CAP scenarios for 2028–2034.

detail.abstract: This article critically analyses the enforcement framework of the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA), with a focus on its early operational phase. The DMA establishes a new regulatory regime that addresses entrenched platform power through ex ante obligations on designated gatekeepers. Building on the European Commission’s emerging practice, ranging from gatekeeper designations and compliance reporting to non-compliance investigations and judicial review, the study examines how Article 3 DMA has been applied in practice. It highlights frictions in the enforcement of core obligations concerning data governance, interoperability, default settings, and app distribution. The analysis further explores the institutional dynamics between the Commission, national authorities, the Digital Markets Advisory Committee, and the High-Level Group, showing how these bodies shape the coherence of DMA enforcement within the broader EU digital acquis. By tracing the regulatory trajectory from designation to compliance, the article assesses whether the DMA can fulfil its stated objectives of fairness and contestability in digital markets, while it also identifies the structural and institutional challenges that may hinder its effectiveness.
