title: Non-Timber Forest Products and Their Role in Sustaining Rural and Tribal Livelihoods in Jharkhand

detail.title: Non-Timber Forest Products and Their Role in Sustaining Rural and Tribal Livelihoods in Jharkhand
detail.abstract: Non timber forest products (NTFPs) are defined as biological resources of plant and animal origin, harvested from natural forests, plantations, wooded land, and trees outside forests (FAO). This paper is an attempt to examines the role of Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) in sustaining rural and tribal livelihoods in Jharkhand. The study employs a descriptive and analytical research design, using secondary data to explore the socioeconomic significance, challenges, and opportunities associated with NTFPs. Key NTFPs identified in Jharkhand include Lac, Sal seeds, Sal leaves, Mahua flowers, Bamboo shoots, Karanj, Kusum, Amla, Tamarind, Palas (Tesuphool), Chironji, Harra, Kendu leaves, Honey, and Dori (Mahua seed oil). The study has been categorized the contributions of NTFPs into two dimensions: first, socioeconomic significance for forest-dependent and tribal communities-consisting livelihood security, household income, poverty reduction, food security, cultural and traditional importance, and women's empowerment; and second, economic impact on the state, including contribution to state revenue, employment generation, rural entrepreneurship, trade and export, and sustainable development. Despite their importance, NTFPs face challenges such as market inefficiencies, inadequate value addition and processing facilities, limited business and marketing skills, and unsustainable harvesting practices. The findings highlight the need for policy support, capacity building, and sustainable management strategies to enhance the economic and social benefits of NTFPs in Jharkhand.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the consumer incidence and targeting efficiency of state sales tax exemptions for feminine hygiene products (FHPs). Using NielsenIQ Retail Scanner and Consumer Panel data, we implement a stacked difference-indifferences event-study design to estimate the effects of tax removal on sales quantities and tax-exclusive prices in states adopting these between 2015 and 2020. detail.abstract:
This paper proposes Universal Catastrophic Coverage with Health Savings Empowerment (UCC/HSE) as a structural replacement for the Affordable Care Act’s subsidy-driven insurance architecture. The central claim is that American health financing should be divided according to the nature of medical risk: catastrophic, unpredictable, high-cost events should be insured through a universal catastrophic layer, while routine and predictable care should be financed through portable, prefunded, consumer-controlled health savings accounts. UCC/HSE replaces open-ended premium-linked subsidies, cost-sharing reductions, exchange administration, and the tax preference for comprehensive employer-sponsored insurance with catastrophic credits, federal HSA deposits, federal reinsurance, and statutory fiscal guardrails.

The model preserves Medicare unchanged and refocuses Medicaid on long-term services and supports, Aged/Blind/Disabled populations, medically complex children, and CHIP continuity. It includes chronic-condition HSA support, pediatric and preventive-care funding, rural hospital stabilization, supplemental-coverage guardrails, and protections against benefit creep. The employer market is not abolished but recomposed: tax-favored premium compensation is gradually redirected toward wages, employer HSA contributions, portable catastrophic coverage, and limited supplemental benefits.

Using a CBO-style scoring framework and MEPS-based catastrophic-spending reconstruction, the paper estimates that UCC/HSE entails a net federal transition cost over the first ten years relative to the ACA baseline, but produces substantial long-run federal savings over twenty- and thirty-year horizons as benchmark-linked catastrophic pricing, fixed HSA formulas, employer-exclusion reform, administrative simplification, and routine-care price discipline compound. The paper argues that UCC/HSE offers a fiscally bounded, market-oriented, and politically cross-cutting framework for universal financial protection without perpetuating the ACA’s open-ended subsidy dynamics, comprehensive-plan inflation, and routine-care price opacity.

title: The National Sovereign AI Readiness Index (NSARI) A Replicable Framework for Measuring Infrastructure-Governance Alignment in Non-Western AI Ecosystems

detail.title: The National Sovereign AI Readiness Index (NSARI) A Replicable Framework for Measuring Infrastructure-Governance Alignment in Non-Western AI Ecosystems

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently.

detail.abstract:
Problem/Motivation: The proliferation of national AI strategies, sovereign cloud programmes, and government foundation model initiatives has created a critical measurement gap in comparative AI governance research: no existing instrument quantifies the structural misalignment between what a nation builds in AI infrastructure and what it governs through regulatory frameworks. Oxford Insights measures government readiness but not infrastructure. Tortoise Media measures capability but conflates commercial and sovereign dimensions. The OECD AI Principles provide normative guidance but not a measurement instrument. This gap makes the Sovereignty Paradox — the condition in which infrastructure investment systematically outpaces governance framework maturity — invisible to comparative analysis and untrackable over time.

Approach/Method: This paper formally introduces the National Sovereign AI Readiness Index (NSARI) as a replicable, citable methodology for measuring infrastructure-governance alignment at the national level. The paper presents the complete formal specification: (1) the composite NSARI formula and five dimension sub-formulae with explicit variable definitions for Infrastructure Sovereignty (IS), Regulatory Maturity (RM), Institutional Capacity (IC), Algorithmic Sovereignty (AS), and Human Capital Readiness (HC); (2) the IS-RM Gap metric with a five-zone interpretive framework; (3) a four-tier evidence hierarchy for consistent cross-jurisdictional scoring; (4) operationalized scoring guidance for all five dimensions across five band levels; (5) an EU calibration validation using Germany, France, and Estonia as benchmark cases; and (6) a nine-step replication protocol enabling independent application by other researchers.

Findings: The EU calibration validation confirms the NSARI's discriminant validity across three critical tests. All three EU member states (Germany, France, Estonia) produce negative IS-RM gaps, consistent with the EU AI Act's statutory framework driving Regulatory Maturity above Infrastructure Sovereignty scores. France's stronger Algorithmic Sovereignty from Mistral AI correctly produces a higher AS score than Germany. Estonia's extreme negative IS-RM gap (−2.8) correctly captures the paradox of the world's most e-governance-advanced state having among the lowest sovereign compute capacity in the EU. All three EU states score materially above the GCC average on Regulatory Maturity (8.6–8.8 vs. GCC average 4.3), confirming the NSARI correctly discriminates between statutory and non-statutory governance regimes across regional contexts.

Practical Implications: The NSARI replication protocol enables any researcher to apply the framework to any national or regional context using publicly available primary sources, producing NSARI-compliant scores comparable to published applications. Annual rescoring produces a longitudinal governance-infrastructure alignment trajectory. Cross-regional extension to ASEAN, the African Union, and Latin America is identified as a priority research direction, to test whether the GCC Sovereignty Paradox documented in Pillai (2026c) is region-specific or globally structural. NSARI version 2.0, incorporating empirically derived dimension weights following primary validation, is proposed as the immediate successor instrument.

title: Basket-Carr: Radon Inversion for Multi-Asset Hedging

detail.title: Basket-Carr: Radon Inversion for Multi-Asset Hedging
detail.abstract: Carr-Madan replication is a Hessian identity. This paper gives its multi-asset analogue for basket calls. Basket calls are primitives of rank-one hyperplane Hessian atoms, and treating the atom offset as a coordinate alongside direction turns multi-asset static replication into filtered Radon inversion on direction-offset space. The resulting coefficient is signed, so finite hedging becomes sparse signed synthesis rather than positive conic spanning. Homogeneous formulas appear as the zero-offset slice of the operator, while non-homogeneous payoffs use the full offset axis. The paper proves the mixed-Hessian and complete-hyperplane obstructions, a finite-variation oracle bound, BLASSO optimality conditions and a composite pricing certificate. On a calibrated two-asset benchmark, a 32-atom Basket-Carr BLASSO hedge improves the 50-atom Bossu-Crepey-Nguyen-style basket-ReLU test RMSE by 1.32% with 36% fewer atoms; debiasing the same support reduces RMSE by 24.6%.

detail.title: The Internet of Things and the circular economy: A systematic literature review and research agenda
detail.abstract: In recent years, the concept of a circular economy (CE) has gained importance and attracted significant attention among scholars and practitioners. Research that examines the role of modern technologies in supporting the transition from a linear economy to the CE is therefore highly needed. This article analyzes and classifies existing research at the intersection of the CE and the Internet of Things (IoT), as an enabling technology. While studies on both concepts have proliferated, there is a lack of research that systematizes the literature and clarifies the relationship between the IoT and the CE. In order to achieve this, we reviewed a total of 170 academic articles published between 2007 and 2021 from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. Based on the coding of keywords, four categories can be identified: (1) IoT-related technologies in the CE context, (2) enablers of IoT in the CE, (3) barriers to IoT adoption in the CE, and (4) the impacts of the IoT on the sustainability of (circular) economies. The current study is the first attempt to use a keyword coding approach to better understand IoT research in the CE domain. The review findings identify important drivers and enablers and provide a structured framework for research in this field. Finally, this study highlights several research directions that may provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners.

detail.abstract: In August 2022, the United States Office of Foreign Assets Control designated Tornado Cash-an autonomous smart contract protocol with no directors, no registered office, and no territorial jurisdiction-as a Specially Designated National. The most territorial of instruments, the sanctions list, was deployed against the most postterritorial of entities. The state won. This article argues that this episode is not an anomaly but a structural revelation: digital sovereignty contains an internal contradiction. The same technologies that decentralise territorial authority simultaneously create new architectures of control that may be more granular, more automated, and more difficult to contest than the territorial sovereignty they displace. Drawing on the regulation of decentralised autonomous organisations, the emergence of central bank digital currencies, extraterritorial sanctions enforcement, platform governance, and digital identity infrastructure, the article traces the mechanisms through which states have adapted to post-territorial governance not by abandoning sovereignty but by relocating it-from the border to the compliance layer, from the passport to the wallet address, from the prison to the frozen account. The article situates this transformation within a broader account of digital infrastructure as the new territory of sovereign power, engages critically with the libertarian origins of the digital sovereignty thesis, and identifies the governance implications of a world in which whoever controls the infrastructure controls the governance.

title: Mapping the Agility-Efficiency Frontier in Supply Chain Network Design A Bi-Objective Pareto Framework for Quantifying the Cost-Resilience Trade-off

detail.title: Mapping the Agility-Efficiency Frontier in Supply Chain Network Design A Bi-Objective Pareto Framework for Quantifying the Cost-Resilience Trade-off
detail.abstract: The Agility-Efficiency Frontier (AEF) was introduced as a conceptual framework representing the trade-off between total network cost and structural resilience in supply chain network design (SCND). That framework has remained schematic: the resilience axis is undefined, no algorithm exists to trace the boundary, and the mechanism by which structural innovations shift the curve has not been formalised. This paper supplies the missing mathematical structure, with deliberate scope limitations. Four contributions are made. First, the AEF is defined as the Pareto boundary of a bi-objective Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP), with the Structural Resilience Index (SRI)-a weighted composite of node redundancy, geographic dispersion, capacity slack, and a temporal resilience proxy-as the second objective. Second, three mathematical properties of the frontier are proved for the LP relaxation: (i) convexity under independent disruption risks; (ii) an upper bound on the resilience gap incurred by deterministic single-objective optimisation; and (iii) monotonicity of each SRI sub-index. Each proof states explicitly where it does and does not extend to the integer programme. Third, the Frontier Shift Operator and its Shift Efficiency Ratio (SE) are defined; a normalisation correction is introduced so that SE is dimensionally consistent across different cost scales. Fourth, the complete framework is demonstrated on a stylised five-facility, six-market instance. Two limitations are stated explicitly. The SRI weight vector is set to equal illustrative values (0.25 each); without industry-specific calibration, the SRI functions as an internal ranking tool and its numerical values carry no cross-industry validity. The Temporal Resilience Proxy (Rt) uses weighted-average lead time as a recovery-time approximation; the assumptions underlying this choice are set out and an alternative maximum-lead-time formulation is noted. Weight calibration and empirical validation are identified as the primary outstanding requirements before the framework can be applied operationally.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a formal architectural distinction between two classes of AI governance systems that has not previously been documented in the literature. Class I systems, designated Reasoning-Process PMCSs, govern cognitive processes that occur within the boundary of a human-AI conversation. Class II systems, designated Execution-Cycle PMCSs, govern the full cycle from cognitive output to world-state change, reaching outside the conversation through external system connections and operating autonomously across a time dimension. The boundary between these classes is structural, not a matter of complexity or sophistication. We specify three architectural invariants that are necessary and sufficient for Class II classification: external system reach, autonomous time dimension, and world-state completion criterion. A system that satisfies all three invariants closes what we term the deployment gap, the structural absence of a governed handoff from AI-assisted cognitive output to real-world product. We argue that this gap is not a capability problem and not a motivation problem. It is an architectural problem that Class I systems are constitutionally unable to close, regardless of their reasoning sophistication. The distinction is derived from and tested against a proof-of-concept system, Einstjii PMCS v1.1, documented as the first Class II system ever constructed. The system reaches outside the conversation through Zapier integration, uses live web search to conduct market intelligence analysis, fires an automated deployment trigger without operator initiation, and defines completion as deployment infrastructure confirmed in the world. It satisfies all three invariants by construction. We provide a classification test, a build standards framework for admitting new systems to the product line, and a falsifiable primary research claim with a defined evidence standard. The paper establishes the architectural boundary as a durable research contribution and opens the execution-cycle governance of human-AI collaboration as a formally bounded research domain.

detail.abstract: Are the growing number of TikTok "bans" prohibited under the Bill of Attainder Clause of the U.S. Constitution? Probably not, but this conclusion is not as obvious as one might think. Accordingly, this brief Article examines one of the most pressing national security issues of the current moment: increasing legislative activity at federal and state levels to ban TikTok, and whether such bans would comport with the Constitution's prohibitions against "bills of attainder." TikTok is a hugely popular social media application owned by ByteDance, a technology company located in the People's Republic of China (PRC). Due to these deep ties to the PRC, a growing number of legislators, governors, and federal government agencies have taken steps to limit the reach of TikTok within the United States on security grounds. The security concerns used to justify the bans fall into two general categories. First, there is the risk of misuse of the personal, demographic, and social data gathered by TikTok. Second, there is the opportunity that TikTok provides to the PRC to disseminate Chinese Communist Party (CCP) propaganda. Within the United States, these concerns pit state and federal government interests against the extensive economic activity of a $400 billion corporate behemoth, making for a potential legal battle of great societal significance. The particularity of these government actions regarding TikTok may seem to raise questions about the Constitution's Bill of Attainder Clause, which is designed to prevent such punishments that arose in an unseemly era of legislative pronouncements of guilt motivated by the caprice of kings and politicians. This Article examines whether TikTok bans would constitute bills of attainder by analyzing Kaspersky Laboratory v. DHS, which reviewed a Congressional ban on using Kaspersky Labs products by the federal government. 1 Kaspersky is a leading case in bill of attainder jurisprudence. It presents a similar fact pattern involving foreign technology and government action to prevent security threats and accordingly has great significance for the current moment. This Article concludes that not only are TikTok bans as currently conceived not bills of attainder (because they do not punish) but also that the ahistorical and atextual judicial expansion of the range of laws covered by the Bill of Attainder Clause may become untenable in an age of complex nation-state competition where nimble legislative interventions for security matters beyond TikTok may become increasingly necessary.

detail.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in operational systems, yet little is known about how advice format shapes human decision making in dynamic, interdependent settings. We study this question in the Beer Game, a canonical supply-chain experiment in which participants repeatedly place orders under delays, local information, and cross-role interdependence. In a live classroom experiment, upstream and downstream supply-chain segments were randomly assigned to no AI, a qualitative AI advisor that provides logic-based guidance, or a quantitative AI advisor that provides numerical recommendations. We found that the qualitative AI improved costs, reduced bullwhip-related behavioral distortions, and moved participants closer to a benchmark ordering policy. Although quantitative AI performed similar to no AI on average, more intense AI engagement led to better outcomes. AI usage also generated spillovers, raising costs for immediate neighbor roles. Our findings suggest that the value of AI depends on advice form, user engagement, and system context. We contribute to the literature by identifying advice specificity as a consequential design choice in human-AI collaboration and by showing that AI deployment in interdependent systems should be evaluated as a workflow design problem, not only as an individual productivity tool.

detail.abstract: Purpose-This research investigates the phenomenon of AI complacency-The employee's tendency to intentionally neglect validating AI-generated output even in the presence of systematic errors. It identifies the lack of monitoring accountability as the underlying driver of this phenomenon, assesses its consequences, and offers strategies for mitigation. Design/methodology/approach-Grounded in contingency theory, this research employs six experimental studies (N 5 1,370 participants), including one study with service employees across industries (N 5 160 participants), to examine how insufficient monitoring accountability facilitates the emergence of AI complacency. The research explores both the causal mechanisms and the boundary conditions that modulate this effect. Findings-The results show that the primary driver of AI complacency is the lack of accountability in monitoring AI-generated outputs. This complacency leads to detrimental work-related outcomes, such as increased commission errors and a diminished willingness to evaluate AI-generated outputs critically. The research also identifies situational factors that exacerbate and buffer these effects. Practical implications-The findings highlight the critical need for organizations to implement systemic accountability frameworks that ensure employees actively engage with and oversee AI-generated output. Originality/value-This research is among the first to examine AI complacency in the context of service provision empirically. It provides a theoretical framework, robust empirical evidence, and practical recommendations for improving Employee-AI collaboration in service provision, contributing to both academic discourse and managerial practice.

detail.abstract:
Traditional economic theory basically says people are rational and always try to make the best choices to get the most out of things. But in real life, that's not always how it goes. People often act in ways that don't match up with that idea.

I think behavioral biases play a big role here, like how loss aversion makes folks hate losing something more than they like gaining it. Or anchoring, where the first price you see sticks in your head and affects everything else. And herd behavior, you know, when everyone follows the crowd without thinking much. These things mess with how consumers make decisions in today's markets.

When you look at purchasing patterns, its clear these biases shape what people buy and why. Pricing seems off sometimes because of them too, like overpaying just because of some initial number. Overall market stuff gets influenced, and it feels like the whole system bends around these psychological quirks.

For businesses, this means they might need to adjust how they market things, maybe using these biases on purpose or not. Policymakers could use it to make better rules. It seems important to mix in these behavioral ideas into economic models, otherwise predicting what consumers will do is just guessing. This part gets a bit messy, but yeah, understanding it better could help a lot.

title: THE EFFECT OF VISUAL AND NARRATIVE CONTENT DESIGN ON CONSUMER PURCHASE INTENTION IN ONLINE SHOPPING ON INSTAGRAM

detail.title: THE EFFECT OF VISUAL AND NARRATIVE CONTENT DESIGN ON CONSUMER PURCHASE INTENTION IN ONLINE SHOPPING ON INSTAGRAM
detail.abstract:
This study examines the effect of visual and narrative content design on consumer purchase intention in online shopping on Instagram. With the rapid growth of social media marketing, Instagram has emerged as one of the most influential platforms for brand promotion, consumer engagement, and online purchasing decisions. The study focuses on how visual elements such as image quality, colour combinations, layout, videos, and design aesthetics, along with narrative elements such as captions, storytelling, emotional appeal, humour, and message clarity, influence consumers’ intention to purchase products online.

The research adopts a quantitative approach using a structured questionnaire distributed through online platforms. A total of 226 valid responses were collected from active Instagram users belonging to different age groups and educational backgrounds. The data was analysed using Microsoft Excel through demographic analysis, mean score analysis, correlation analysis, hypothesis testing, and standard deviation analysis.

The findings reveal that both visual and narrative content significantly influence consumer purchase intention on Instagram. Visual content showed a strong positive correlation with purchase intention (0.749), while narrative content also demonstrated a strong positive relationship (0.746). However, the combined effect of visual and narrative content showed the highest influence on purchase intention with a correlation value of 0.787. The study concludes that consumers are more likely to engage with and purchase products when visually appealing content is supported by effective storytelling and clear communication.

The research highlights the importance of integrated content strategies for marketers, influencers, and businesses using Instagram as a promotional platform. The study contributes to existing literature by combining visual and narrative dimensions within a single framework and provides practical recommendations for designing effective Instagram marketing content.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has generated high expectations regarding future productivity growth. This paper situates such expectations in the historical lineage of the Solow productivity paradox and later J-curve interpretations of technological change. We distinguish between ex-ante expectations formed during the 1970s-1980s computer era, ex-post outcomes observed in the 1990s-2000s, and a newer interpretation associated with hidden costs of the internet era. We argue that AI may compress some adjustment lags because it enters an already digitalized economy, yet may intensify distributional tensions. Recent empirical evidence from both optimists and skeptics is surveyed to illuminate the range of outcomes now under debate. This revised edition incorporates new perspectives from organizational theory, political economy, heterodox ecology, and cultural critique-asking what happens to J-curve dynamics when AI platforms decay, when media amplify hype, when oligopoly concentrates rents, and when alternative wellbeing metrics challenge GDP as the measure of progress. The broader lesson remains temporal and distributional: productivity gains may emerge eventually, but workers and households bear present costs immediately.

detail.title: Impact of lottery promotion wins and losses: evidence from a promotion in a mobile payment service
detail.abstract: Purpose-Lottery promotion is a gambled price discount that provides random incentives for each consumer transaction. This study investigates how winning (i.e. being selected exactly once during the promotion) and losing (i.e. never being selected) influence consumer payment both during and after the promotion. Design/methodology/approach-Using data from a lottery promotion conducted by a Japanese mobile payment provider, we applied a difference-indifferences with propensity score weighting approach. By comparing winners and losers, respectively, to non-participants, we estimated the causal effects of winning and losing on consumer payment during and after the promotion. Findings-The results show that, during the promotion, even those who lost the lottery increased their payment amounts compared to non-participants and winners demonstrated a larger increase than losers. Furthermore, after the promotion, losing still led to higher payment amounts relative to non-participation, while winning produced an even greater increase than losing. Originality/value-Few previous studies have focused on the losing effect, used non-participants as a baseline or examined the post-promotion period. This study fills an important research gap by identifying and comparing the causal effects of winning and losing on consumer payment during and after the promotion. Academically, it extends uncertainty resolution theory to scenarios involving losses and provides empirical evidence for habit formation driven by the promotion experience, independent of incentive receipt. By discussing these effects, this paper also provides comprehensive insights into the cost-effectiveness and design of lottery promotions and offers significant practical implications.

title: The Hidden Subsidy: How Cheap Time Supports Cash Prices in Inconvenient Markets

detail.title: The Hidden Subsidy: How Cheap Time Supports Cash Prices in Inconvenient Markets
detail.abstract: Economists have long recognized that time-poor consumers pay premiums for convenience. Delivery, priority service, one-click purchasing, and reduced search effort all command higher prices because buyers with high opportunity costs of time are willing to pay to avoid delay and hassle. This paper examines the mirror-image phenomenon in raw, unbundled, and inconvenient markets. In settings such as pickup-only furniture listed on Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, estate-sale goods, scrap materials, roadside produce, and similar low-service transactions, low-time-value buyers do more than hunt for bargains. They can serve as the marginal participants who sustain the visible cash price by absorbing hidden time, travel, loading, scheduling, and hassle costs that high-time-value buyers refuse to bear. The paper identifies this as a hidden subsidy: the seller receives a cash price that appears to reflect the market value of the good, while the buyer quietly supplies the missing convenience through cheap time and personal effort. Without these buyers, the seller would likely have to lower the cash price, provide delivery or other convenience services, or accept unsold inventory. Because the time component is private, heterogeneous, and usually invisible, the observed sticker price can become a misleading reference point for broader market perceptions. This paper situates the mechanism against the literature on search costs, convenience premiums, and price dispersion, and argues that low-time-value consumers are not always price-eroding bargain hunters. In inconvenient physical markets, they may also be unwitting supporters of seller cash revenue.

title: Reconsidering the (co)creation of value. A critical review of product, service and customer dominant logics and a proposal for a new, value attribution logic.

detail.title: Reconsidering the (co)creation of value. A critical review of product, service and customer dominant logics and a proposal for a new, value attribution logic.
detail.abstract: In this conceptual paper I propose after a critical literature review that value, for any actor, should be considered a dynamic attribution to services instead of the output of creation or cocreation. This proposal marks the start of the development of a new, Value Attribution Logic (VAL), which does not take the Product or Service Dominant Logic (PDL or SDL) as its reference and neither the customer, but every economic interactor in its primary role of wannabe beneficiary from the exchange of service-for-services. In this role, everyone is looking for opportunities to maintain, improve or replace systems for which responsibility is felt. Five foundational VAL axioms are introduced and compared with those of SDL. This comparison reveals that SDL is more similar to PDL than initially thought. It also explains why other value logics, such as Service Logic and Customer Dominant Logic have been proposed later. However, the belief that value cumulates and is embedded in something also shores these logics. VAL abandons value thingification, but remains loyal to service thinking, without allowing it to dominate. Implications for research and marketing practice are discussed extensively.

detail.abstract: Dorian Lazzari proposed the Cubish address system, which divides the Earth into 5.1 trillion cubes and assigns each cube a unique identifier, thereby enabling precise connections between the physical and digital worlds (Lazzari, 2025; Digital Digest, 2025). This vision goes beyond the limitations of traditional flat maps that merely indicate location, offering the possibility of structuring space with precision and mapping the digital and physical worlds one-to-one. This paper takes Lazzari's proposal as a starting point and expands it to explore a new framework that integrates space, time, and activity. Specifically, it introduces the concept of a three-dimensional activity map and an operating system (OS) that manages it. By incorporating a precise time axis based on GPS atomic clocks, the paper suggests a structure in which reality and virtuality operate as "a single computational system." Furthermore, it discusses the potential social transition in which national sovereignty shifts from territory to OS-centered control, and envisions a new paradigm of an information-based society by establishing a foundation for mapping the metaverse and digital twins one-to-one with the real world (Lee, 2026a; Lee, 2026b).

title: Dynamic Scheduling of a Parallel-Server Queueing System: A Computational Method for High-Dimensional Problems

detail.title: Dynamic Scheduling of a Parallel-Server Queueing System: A Computational Method for High-Dimensional Problems
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: A key operational challenge for call centers is to decide, in real time, which waiting customer should be served by which available agent. This is known as skill-based routing, and the decision becomes especially difficult in large systems with many customer classes, where standard dynamic programming methods can be computationally intractable. 

Methodology/results: Focusing on the Halfin-Whitt heavy-traffic regime and an infinite-horizon discounted cost criterion, we develop a computational method that scales to high-dimensional settings with many customer classes. Our approach begins by deriving an approximating diffusion control problem in the heavy traffic limiting regime. Building on earlier work by Han et al. (2018), we develop a simulation-based method to solve this problem, relying heavily on deep neural network techniques. Using this framework, we construct a policy for the original (prelimit) call center scheduling problem. To evaluate performance, we adopt a data-driven approach. Using call center data from a large U.S. bank, we calibrate the model and construct realistic test instances. We then compare the resulting policy with benchmark policies drawn from the literature. Across all test problems considered so far, our policy performs at least as well as or better than the best benchmark identified. Moreover, the method remains computationally feasible in dimensions up to 100, corresponding to call centers with 100 or more distinct customer classes. 

Managerial implications: The proposed approach gives managers a scalable way to improve real-time routing decisions in complex service systems. It can help call centers improve service quality and evaluate routing policies before implementing them. More broadly, the paper provides decision makers with a computational framework for studying and managing high-dimensional service systems that are too large for standard exact methods.

title: The 5-Star Accountability System: A Conceptual Framework for Organizational Discipline, Productivity, and Ethical Governance in India

detail.title: The 5-Star Accountability System: A Conceptual Framework for Organizational Discipline, Productivity, and Ethical Governance in India
detail.abstract: Organizations and public institutions in India continuously face challenges relating to professional misconduct, corruption, absenteeism, negligence, weak accountability systems, declining productivity, and inconsistent disciplinary procedures. Traditional disciplinary mechanisms are often reactive, delayed, or excessively bureaucratic, resulting in reduced organizational efficiency and declining public trust. This paper introduces the "5-Star Accountability System," a conceptual accountability framework designed to improve organizational discipline, employee responsibility, ethical governance, and workplace productivity. Under this framework, every employee begins with five stars representing full organizational trust and professional credibility. Each verified instance of professional misconduct or policy violation results in the deduction of one star through a structured review mechanism. The system functions progressively by providing employees opportunities for behavioural correction before severe disciplinary actions are imposed. At the fourth violation stage, employees may either continue under strict organizational restrictions or voluntarily resign with limited benefits. Reaching the fifth violation results in termination without benefits. The paper argues that the proposed framework may improve transparency, workplace culture, public trust, administrative efficiency, and employee behaviour in both Government Service Sectors and Corporate Institutions. The study is conceptual in nature and is based on the Indian organizational and administrative context.

title: Does Democratization Reduce Inequality? A Critical Appraisal of the Middle-Ground Theory
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC) and New York University (NYU) - Department of Politics

detail.title: Does Democratization Reduce Inequality? A Critical Appraisal of the Middle-Ground Theory
detail.abstract: Arguing against prior theories that democratization has no impact on income inequality, Dorsch and Maarek (2019) contend in an APSR article that democratization causes extreme income distributions to move towards a "middle ground," reducing inequality in highly unequal autocracies while increasing inequality in relatively egalitarian ones. Central to the study's evidence is an instrumental variable strategy that leverages the regional share of democracies, and its interaction with initial inequality levels, to identify both the effect of democratization and the democracy-inequality interaction. We provide a critical replication of this study, making two central contributions. First, we show that the generated instrument violates the exclusion restriction and, second, even when properly constructed, the same linear function cannot be used to identify two causal effects. We then demonstrate how the same source of exogenous variation can be used to identify multiple causal effects using a generalized additive model, with non-linearities in the first stages serving as additional instruments. Across all specifications, the data do not support the middle-ground theory proposed by the authors: neither democracy nor its interaction with initial inequality has a statistically significant effect on the Gini coefficient. Our findings are consistent with an extensive literature in economics and political science that has struggled to uncover a systematic democracy-inequality link. The replication method we employ offers a practical tool for other studies in contexts where valid instruments are scarce or the exclusion restriction is difficult to satisfy.

detail.abstract: A leading rationale for restricting stablecoins is the argument that stablecoins are run-prone, and that stablecoin runs will impose negative externalities via contagious loss of confidence. A critical examination shows that the evidence of run-and panic-proneness in the antebellum US private banknote system is unrepresentative of minimally restricted banknote systems around the globe, and is not relevant to stablecoins. The most prominent stablecoin run (on USDC in 2023) did not exhibit contagion. A second concern is that because stablecoin prices deviate from par, their use as media of exchange is inefficient. A more comprehensive perspective finds that inefficiency does not follow from non-par pricing. The US "GENIUS Act" (signed into law July 2025) restricts dollar stablecoins in ways that harm stablecoin users. The restrictions embodied in the act are better explained by rent-seeking than by a search for efficiency.

detail.abstract: This research aims at answering a key question in entrepreneurship studies-whether prior business knowledge is a key factor for start-up success or it is possible to compensate the lack thereof through hands-on experience and in-depth product knowledge. Through an extensive review of international academic literature on the subject and empirical evidence from Uzbekistan's dynamically developing start-up community, the research puts forward three main propositions. Firstly, prior business knowledge (educational and managerial experience, as well as know-how in specific industries) significantly decreases the probability of failure in the early stages of start-up development, especially the first two-three years. Secondly, domain knowledge (knowledge of the particular industry without business education) serves as a partial substitute for prior business knowledge in the process of product development; however, it fails to provide necessary skills in finance and marketing, as well as in scaling up operations. Thirdly, in the absence of institutionalization, a Finance-Marketing Integration Gap (FMIG) serves as a multiplying factor for knowledge deficiencies in underdeveloped markets like Uzbekistan. The research uses the KECCT model (Knowledge, Experience, Competence, Characteristics, Team), presents original tables and visuals, and develops a Contextualised Human Capital Model for entrepreneurship in emerging markets.

detail.title: The Intangible Gap
detail.abstract: We document a large and rising intangible investment gap between small and large U.S. firms. Smaller firms invest disproportionately in intangible capital, despite facing tighter financing constraints, and this gap has tripled since the 1980s alongside a pronounced increase in intangible investment volatility. We develop a dynamic industry-equilibrium model in which firms invest in both physical and intangible capital under financial frictions. Intangible investment is subject to idiosyncratic quality shocks and can be partially financed internally through equity-based compensation. These features generate an optionlike payoff to intangible investment: downside risk is limited by exit, while upside gains scale with realized quality. This mechanism makes intangible capital particularly attractive for small firms with high exit risk. Our analysis reveals that the joint increase in intangible investment volatility and the decline in financing frictions for intangible capital account for approximately 60% of the post-2000 gap in intangible-to-physical capital ratios between small and large firms over the 2001-2023 period.

detail.title: Ownership, governance mechanisms, and business model design
detail.abstract: Using the trade-off theory of operating leverage to measure exchange value and accounting data to assess the effectiveness of value capture, this article examines how ownership and governance mechanisms influence business model design. Based on 68,745 firm-year observations of Polish enterprises, the results show that joint-stock companies develop the most technologically advanced business models and generate the highest exchange value. However, they are also the least effective in capturing this value. These firms are likely among the most innovation-intensive, yet their innovativeness does not translate into shareholder value. In contrast, unlimited liability companies employ the least technologically advanced business models and generate relatively low exchange value, but they are highly effective in capturing it. Cooperatives, meanwhile, create limited exchange value and are inefficient in capturing it. Most likely, were it not for their mission of providing non-financial benefits to members, they would lack a sustainable basis for operation.

detail.abstract: This paper critically examines the role of the U.S. Supreme Court under Chief Justice John Roberts in enabling a structural decline in democratic norms and facilitating the consolidation of authoritarian political power. Through analysis of landmark rulings-Citizens United v. FEC (2010), Shelby County v. Holder (2013), Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), Trump v. United States (2024), and Louisiana v. Callais (2026)this paper demonstrates how the Roberts Court has systematically dismantled institutional safeguards against corruption, voter suppression, civil rights erosion, and unchecked executive authority. Rather than arguing direct causation between individual rulings and electoral outcomes, the paper advances a structural argument: that the Roberts Court has created and sustained the legal architecture within which authoritarian consolidation becomes durable and self-reinforcing. The ethical conduct of Justice Clarence Thomas further compromises the Court's institutional legitimacy. Drawing on empirical data and legal analysis, and situating the Court's jurisprudence within the broader democratic backsliding literature, this paper argues that the Roberts Court has not merely failed to protect democracy - it has actively constructed the conditions for its erosion.

title: 60 horas de nadie

detail.title: 60 horas de nadie
detail.abstract: El problema invisible Imagina esta situación: un miembro de tu equipo recibe una tarea. La estimación acordada es de 40 horas. Semanas después, cuando la tarea está completada, el tiempo real invertido ha sido de 200 horas. La diferencia, 160 horas, no desaparece. Y nadie sabe muy bien qué hacer con ella. Esa incertidumbre es el origen de una cadena de injusticias que, en muchos equipos, se repite de forma silenciosa y sistemática. No por mala voluntad de nadie, sino porque las reglas con las que se gestiona el trabajo no están diseñadas para manejar esa complejidad. Este artículo analiza ese problema, lo formula con precisión y propone un sistema de compensación que alinea los incentivos del equipo de forma justa y sostenible. Al final, aborda también el coste humano de no resolverlo, y por qué ese coste es hoy mayor que nunca.

title: **AI-Driven Crypto Trust Trajectories: Financial Stability, Electronic Payments Integration, and Policy Framework for Emerging Mar kets**

detail.title: **AI-Driven Crypto Trust Trajectories: Financial Stability, Electronic Payments Integration, and Policy Framework for Emerging Mar kets**
detail.abstract: This study examines the convergence of artificial intelligence and crypto assets as dual forces reshaping financial stability in emerging markets. Drawing on Bank of England, FSB, and IMF frameworks, we project institutional trust in crypto assets reaching **75% by 2030**, contingent upon MiCA-style regulatory harmonization, mandatory stablecoin reserve transparency, and robust AI model governance. Public adoption lags at **55%**, constrained by price volatility, regulatory uncertainty, and user experience friction. Electronic payments infrastructure emerges as the **primary trust accelerator**, potentially reducing adoption barriers by 60%. Key findings refute binary traditional-vs-digital banking conflict, identifying **evolutionary complementarity**. Stablecoins demonstrate increasing reliance on legacy financial reserves (USDC: 100% cash-backed). HKIMR-relevant policy recommendations include AI-crypto regulatory sandboxes, cross-border stablecoin standards, and digital payment gateway frameworks. Mixed-methods analysis combines policy document review, Chainalysis adoption metrics, and logistic growth modeling calibrated on 2020-2026 data.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether environmental enforcement changes stock prices in Brazil. I combine IBAMA infraction notices, market and accounting data, and handcurated environmental news involving listed firms. The design is a causal financial event study: daily abnormal returns are compared with a contemporaneous Control Group, and the cumulative abnormal return is the sum of daily treatment effects. Average official IBAMA notices do not generate a robust negative response. Notices classified as having significant environmental impact and strict environmental news events produce economically large negative cumulative abnormal returns, with small-sample caveats. The evidence suggests that Brazilian investors do not mechanically price the average administrative enforcement record; they react when environmental information is material, public, or both.

detail.abstract: Some of you might have grown up with the book series "Choose your own Adventure." Well, PROSPER is the adult version. Most contemporary recommender systems blend multiple input signals into a single objective function. Stated user preferences become one feature among many. This paper describes a different architecture, deployed in the PROSPER career intelligence platform, in which user-provided signals are organized into a strict hierarchy. Stated context governs which stated preferences are allowed to constrain the output. Stated preferences always override inferred preferences. The architecture introduces what I call a value-alignment guardrail, meaning a deterministic gating layer interposed between an inference engine and a downstream large language model that enforces the primacy of user agency over algorithmic adjacency. The system was implemented as part of a workforce-displacement recommendation for serving displaced and transitioning workers in Michigan. It closes a class of failure modes in which inferred adjacencies override the user's declared situation. The clearest example is a displaced worker who has stated they need to remain in their current industry, but who receives recommendations to change industries entirely. I position this approach within the literature on contestable AI, stated-preference primacy in welfare economics, and recent alignment work on user-controlled recommendation. I argue that for high-stakes decision-support systems in workforce, healthcare, and public-benefit domains, the dominant blended-signal paradigm can be improved. Hierarchical signal governance is both technically tractable and ethically warranted.

title: The Economics of the Tariff Chaos in the United States

detail.title: The Economics of the Tariff Chaos in the United States
detail.abstract: This paper examines the economic and institutional consequences of the tariff measures introduced by the second Trump administration under emergency authorities, focusing on the legal and economic instability generated by the resulting "tariff chaos." It traces the evolution of the administration's tariff strategy from the 2025 "Liberation Day" reciprocal tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to the subsequent attempt to reestablish broad-based tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 following adverse rulings by the U.S. courts. The paper argues that the reciprocal tariff program was economically flawed in a fundamental sense because it treated bilateral trade imbalances as evidence of unfair trade and sought to eliminate them through tariffs. In a multilateral trading system characterized by globally fragmented production and complex capital flows, there is no economic rationale for balanced bilateral trade with every partner. Meanwhile, the Section 122 tariff, which is framed in the language of responses to Bretton Woods-era "balance of payments" crises, has been an economic anachronism since the collapse of the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system in 1971, rendering the substance of the litigation economically meaningless. The paper then situates the current tariff turmoil within the broader historical evolution of globalization. Modern globalization is primarily due to the international unbundling of production through global value chains enabled by technological developments including containerization, air cargo transport, information technology, and supply chain management systems. In this context, the stability and predictability of market access conditions become pivotal because firms make highly specific sunk-cost investments in international production networks. The paper draws on the literature on investment under uncertainty to argue that volatile and legally contested tariff regimes increase the "real option value of waiting," discourage new investment, and redirect resources toward non-productive compliance and litigation activities. While hysteresis effects may slow the decline of trade flows, prolonged trade policy instability inevitably alters the geography of trade and investment by disintermediating unstable jurisdictions from global production systems, including by weakening the credibility and value of trade agreements with such jurisdictions.

title: Nauru in the Modern Eye: The Story of the Failed Pacific Island State

detail.title: Nauru in the Modern Eye: The Story of the Failed Pacific Island State
detail.abstract: The Republic of Nauru is a profound study of what happens when a country is given a finite resource and uses all of it. Going from being the world's wealthiest nation by capita to its current state of economic bankruptcy and environmental ruin. The paper Nauru in the Modern Eye: The Story of the Failed Pacific Island State, researches the direction the island went from gaining independence in 1968 to its current state. With a historical and economic analysis, the research present shows that the rapid decline of Nauru was not because they ran out of phosphate, but rather the product of large-scale financial mismanagement and the commodification of sovereignty. This study explores the “Golden Age” of a time when the entire economy relied on phosphate, the collapse of the Nauru Phosphates Royalties Trust, and the modern day host for an Australian refugee center. From looking at the 1965 rejection of relocation to Curtis Island, the paper highlights the commitment to sovereignty of the Nauruan people and how this left the nation completely reliant on foreign aid and controversial international relations. In the end, Nauru serves as a warning above all else for the modern era: a testament to the dangers of not only relying on one source of income but to poor financial decisions and how wealth can be gained at the cost of one's nation.

detail.abstract: Standard economic intuition suggests that ownership should increase care because owners internalize the residual value of an asset. This paper proposes a behavioral qualification to that prediction. When deterioration is gradual and internally absorbed, individuals may underweight depreciation; when deterioration is externally evaluated and discretely penalized, as in leasing arrangements, the same type of loss may become more salient. The paper develops a simple model distinguishing internally absorbed depreciation from externally enforced depreciation. The model generates a counterintuitive prediction: maintenance effort may be lower under ownership than under leasing when deterioration is continuous, incremental, and weakly salient. The framework yields testable predictions regarding salience, inspection, damage structure, experience, and repeated interaction. Rather than reporting new empirical evidence, the paper offers a conceptual mechanism and outlines empirical strategies for future work.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Sequence of Decisions Risk as a proposed governance variable within increasingly complex financial and organizational systems. While modern finance formalized Sequence of Returns Risk as a function of market timing, this framework proposes that materially inferior outcomes may also emerge when otherwise-correct decisions occur in the wrong order. The paper argues that increasing specialization has improved technical expertise while simultaneously fragmenting coordination, sequencing responsibility, and implementation governance across interacting domains. As a result, modern systems may experience recurring structural inefficiencies arising from sequencing failure, dependency disruption, implementation latency, and optionality destruction. To address this problem, the paper introduces a conceptual governance framework incorporating Interaction Complexity, Coordination Drag, Trigger Event Cascades, Irreversibility Risk, and The Z-Axis governance architecture. While initially observed through physician wealth systems, the framework proposes broader applicability across organizational, institutional, and AI-enabled environments characterized by specialization and interaction-sensitive outcomes. This paper is intended as a conceptual and theoretical framework rather than an empirically validated predictive model. Future research may explore governance measurement, sequencing-loss quantification, and coordination dynamics across complex systems.

detail.abstract: When industrial policy reshapes the geography of production, what unpriced amenity travels along? I document this wedge in the post-2018 reshoring of semiconductor manufacturing to the U.S. and partner economies. Zero of 18 state and federal incentive packages for major 2020-2024 fab projects contain a provision tied to basin water scarcity, more-exposed firms shift portfolios toward higher-water-stress basins, and the post-2018 reshoring episode moves 68-219 Mm 3 per year of withdrawal into water-stressed sites globally. A structural location-choice model shows that a Pigouvian water charge within the observed CHIPS-grant range raises the U.S.-plus-ally fab share by 7 percentage points at $5 billion per WRI unit with displaced fabs moving to wetter allies, so pricing basin scarcity at the bidding stage internalizes the wedge without sacrificing reshoring.
